title: The residency cliff: the sign of context trimming's prefill cost flips with serving concurrency
statement: Replay the card paper's recorded mini-SWE-agent trajectories (fallback: the Complexity Trap's released SWE-agent trajectories, HF dataset JetBrains-Research/the-complexity-trap, per the W43 kill record) through one open engine (vLLM or SGLang, prefix cache on, least-recently-used eviction) as $N$ closed-loop sessions that each wait $W$ seconds between calls, for $N \in \{8, 16, 32, 64, 128\}$, $W \in \{0, 20\}$ s and two KV budgets $B$ (full device, half device), under four serializations of the same recorded histories: identity (the Eager arm), per-turn masking $L_5$ re-applied to Eager's recorded history, the recorded Mask-5 trajectories, and an edit-on-miss oracle that applies $L_5$ only on the calls the server reports as cache misses (the server's per-request cached-token count is the input the paper's $L_5$ never sees, card information_asymmetry (2)). Read, from the server counters, the hit fraction $h = T_{\mathrm{hit}} / T_{\mathrm{prompt}}$, executed prefill $T_{\mathrm{uncached}}$ per task, prefill and decode seconds, and tasks per GPU-hour, and test the one-line law that $h$ collapses from its single-tenant value to the shared-system-prompt share once the sessions' working sets no longer fit: $$h(N) \approx h_1\,\mathbb{1}[N \bar s \le B] + h_{\mathrm{sys}}\,\mathbb{1}[N \bar s > B],$$ where $h_1$ is the single-request hit fraction (0.96 for Eager, 0.53 for Mask-5, card sec. 4.3), $h_{\mathrm{sys}}$ the share of a prompt that is the system prompt every session re-references, $\bar s$ a session's peak resident context in KV bytes (peak prompt tokens times the engine's KV bytes per token), and $\mathbb{1}[\cdot]$ the indicator. Step 0 ($0) computes from the trajectories alone: $\bar s$ per serialization, the exact longest-common-prefix executed prefill (which also splits the paper's +608.5% into its fixed-sequence cache term and its trajectory term, card weakest_component (2)), the LRU stack-distance prediction of $h(N, B)$, and $N \bar s / B$ for the rollout configurations FlashNext-RL (2610.28998: 1,024 rollouts, 131,072-token limit, three inference nodes) and MISA-T (2608.11152) publish.
claim: The sign of a context policy's executed-prefill cost is a property of the serving regime, not of the policy: below the residency cliff $N \bar s = B$ per-turn trimming multiplies recomputed prefill, above it trimming is the only policy that reduces it, and the rollout configurations agentic-RL systems papers publish sit above the cliff.
trick: Run the same agent transcripts through one server as more and more simultaneous sessions and watch for the point where the prefix cache can no longer hold them all: below it, dropping old observations every turn multiplies the prefill the server recomputes; above it, every session recomputes its whole prompt anyway and dropping observations is the only thing that saves any.
why_now: The card paper (2610.34763, 2026-10-26) is the first to measure executed prefill, KV time-area and joules for context policies and to write the masking penalty as $-75.1\mathrm{k} + 135.9\mathrm{k}\cdot\rho$ tokens per attempt with $\rho$ the reuse fraction a runtime serves (sec. 5), then leave $\rho$ at its single-request ceiling: 'batching, cache pressure, and cloud GPUs remain untested' (sec. 7). Three papers in the last eleven weeks supply the other half without the context-policy axis: 2610.22863 (2026-10-16) replays Microsoft M365 traces under KV budgets and finds 'at one tenth of the busiest hour's demand, LRU eviction makes 63% of Deep Research calls recompute' (abstract, fetched); MISA-T (2608.11152, 2026-08-11) builds 'residency-time-aware KV accounting' and admission for mixed RL rollouts because 'KV-residency times create substantially different serving demands' (abstract, fetched); WAKMan (2610.36355, 2026-10-26) finds 'agentic steps return within seconds and favor recency' and that one workload parameter flips the best eviction policy (abstract, fetched). Enabling pieces: open engines return per-request cached-token counts (vLLM and SGLang usage fields, the counters the card reads), and released trajectory corpora (the card's artifacts at github.com/sysevol-ai/CodeNib; the Complexity Trap tarballs; Open-SWE-Traces 2606.16038). The law itself is the 1970 stack-distance result for LRU under a cyclic reference pattern (Mattson, Gecsei, Slutz and Traiger); nothing newer is needed, and that is recorded as the flag.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 ($0, 2 days): from the recorded trajectories compute per serialization (identity, $L_5$ re-applied, recorded Mask-5, $L_{10}$ for the Complexity Trap window) the per-call prompt token sequence, the exact longest-common-prefix hit tokens at $N = 1$ (reproducing the card's 96% and 53%), the peak working set $\bar s$ in tokens, and an LRU stack-distance simulation of $h(N, B)$ with the engine's block size; compute $N \bar s / B$ for FlashNext-RL and MISA-T from their stated batch, context limit, inference GPU count and model KV layout. Step 1 (replay, about 50 GPU-hours on one 80 GB H100, or the DGX Spark the card used): serve a 27B-class open model in FP8 (the card's Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 or a smaller stand-in; KV bytes per token read from the server config) with prefix caching on; drive $N$ closed-loop sessions, each sending its recorded prompts in order, decoding to the recorded output length with content discarded, then idling $W$ seconds; sweep $N \in \{8, 16, 32, 64, 128\}$, $W \in \{0, 20\}$ s, $B \in \{B_{\mathrm{full}}, B_{\mathrm{full}}/2\}$, four serializations, two seeded session orderings; about 90 sweep points at 20-40 minutes each. Record per request the server's cached-token count and prompt tokens, prefill and decode wall seconds, and per sweep point tasks per GPU-hour. Readouts: $h(N)$ per arm against the step-0 prediction; the crossover $N^{\times}$ where the $L_5$ arm's executed prefill falls below the identity arm's; the throughput ratio Mask-5 : Eager below and above the cliff; the edit-on-miss oracle as the bound on what cache-aware edit scheduling (CADOC, TokenPilot, Self-GC) recovers in each regime; the prefill share of GPU seconds per regime (a readout for CL-W43-07).
killing_experiment.kills_if: At $N = 128$, $W = 20$ s and $B = B_{\mathrm{full}}/2$, the identity (Eager) arm's hit fraction stays above 0.55 (the card's break-even) and the $L_5$ arm's executed prefill stays above the identity arm's: the LRU prefix cache holds agent working sets through tool waits at every concurrency a single engine runs, the trimming penalty is regime-independent, residency shows up only as admission queueing and never as recompute, the claim's rollout mechanism is dead, and the card's single-tenant number is the deployment number (a citable footnote: 2610.22863's 63% recompute is a fleet-placement effect, not a per-engine one). Dead as a law but kept as a measurement if a crossover exists but sits more than a factor of 2 from $B / \bar s$ at both budgets. The third clause of the claim dies on its own if step 0 puts both published rollout configurations below $N \bar s / B = 1$.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.55 for the full set, 0.75 for the cliff alone: the identity arm's hit fraction falls from about 0.9 to below 0.4 within a factor of 2 in $N$ around $N^* = B / \bar s$ (for a 27B-class FP8 model on 80 GB and SWE-bench Verified sessions peaking near 15k tokens, step 0 puts $N^*$ in the tens of sessions per GPU; the exact number is read, not guessed); above the cliff the $L_5$ arm's executed prefill is 25-35% below the identity arm's (the prompt-volume gap, 150.5k vs 225.6k tokens per attempt, card Table 2) and its tasks per GPU-hour 1.2-1.5x higher, while below the cliff it is 0.6-0.75x (the card's +36.9% wall time); the edit-on-miss oracle matches the better arm in each regime; and FlashNext-RL's published configuration (1,024 rollouts at up to 131k tokens over three inference nodes) sits above $N \bar s / B = 1$ unless its engine offloads KV.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: Stable residency. Card sec. 5: the masking penalty is first-order $-75.1\mathrm{k} + 135.9\mathrm{k}\cdot\rho$ and sec. 7: 'Results cover two stacks on one DGX Spark serving one request at a time; batching, cache pressure, and cloud GPUs remain untested.' CADOC sec. 3.2 (W43 kill record): 'We assume stable prefix caching, no retrieval, and an indefinitely continuing stream.' TurnCost sec. 7: providers 'evict them after a time-to-live, and lose reuse when requests move between backends, none of which we model.' The serving-cost lane's verdict (card, CADOC, TokenPilot, 2607.12161) is therefore 'keep the history, the cache is cheap'; the RL systems side (FlashNext-RL abstract) reports tokens per second per GPU and iteration minutes with no hit fraction at all.
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: If the cliff is where the law puts it and published rollouts sit above it: the 'trimming costs more' results are single-tenant results that do not transfer to RL rollouts, every context-management cost column needs its regime ($N \bar s / B$) stated, agentic-RL rollout concurrency per GPU is sized by $B / \bar s$ or the context policy is chosen to move the cliff, and MISA-T-style admission and observation masking become the same lever seen from two sides. If no cliff appears within a single engine's reach: residency binds through admission queueing rather than recompute, the card's number is the deployment number, and CL-W43-12's rollout half is reworded from prefill to idle sessions (FlashNext-RL's 'a third of sessions idle').

scorecard.target_value: In print: card sec. 7 lists batching and cache pressure as untested and sec. 5 leaves $\rho$ unmeasured; 2610.22863 (abstract): 'About 80% of context tokens are served from the prefix cache' in production and LRU makes 63% of calls recompute at one tenth of peak demand; MISA-T (abstract): rollout sessions' 'KV-residency times create substantially different serving demands'; WAKMan (abstract): 'even a single workload parameter can flip the winner'. Who pays: RL infrastructure teams sizing rollout sessions per GPU (FlashNext-RL, MISA-T, prime-rl and verl users); harness teams choosing a context default for training rollouts versus API serving; the systems groups (CADOC, TokenPilot, AKV, SmoothAgent) whose 'protect the cache' motivation is regime-bound; anyone reporting an executed-prefill or dollar column for a context policy.

impact_ceiling.floor: A regime label on the card's and CADOC's results ('single-tenant') plus the measured cliff on one engine, one model and one budget; a footnote the context-cost papers cite. Requires step 0 and the sweep at one budget. Judgment p 0.40.
impact_ceiling.middle: The cliff law validated on two engines (vLLM, SGLang) and two budgets, the $N \bar s / B$ ruler applied to the published rollout configurations, and a recipe consequence (trim above the cliff, admit below it) adopted as a default in one open RL framework's rollout configuration. Requires step 1 plus a second engine (about 30 more GPU-hours). Judgment p 0.35.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: Every context-management evaluation reports executed prefill with its regime; rollout concurrency in agentic RL is sized by the residency cliff; the lane's cost accounting splits into a below-cliff (cache-priced) and an above-cliff (prefill-priced) regime with one crossover number per model and device. Requires a live RL run instrumented at the rollout engine (lab position) and a second workload family (browsing agents). Judgment p 0.15.

scorecard.relevance: L3 route (Lloyd / Netravali / Tri Dao): direct, the cost structure of agentic serving and rollout engines under cache reuse. L2: moderate, the rollout cost of agentic RL (the claim's training half). L4: direct for the measurement register, every compaction cost column gets a regime label; zero for recipes. L1: small (cost-per-task reporting). Industry: direct (RL infra defaults, harness defaults for training versus serving). Jacob's edge: high in computer engineering (stack-distance cache analysis, GPU memory arithmetic, a one-line law with a sharp transition); theoretical physics not needed. Zero: L5.
scorecard.kill_probe: Step 0 at $0 (2 days), then one replay sweep: about 50 GPU-hours on one H100 (about $150), 5 days; dead if the identity arm's hit fraction stays above 0.55 and $L_5$'s executed prefill stays above identity's at $N = 128$, $W = 20$ s, $B = B_{\mathrm{full}}/2$.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: Counted 2026-11-01 on the arXiv API: Q1 (prefix or KV cache AND agent AND concurrency / multi-tenant / cache pressure / eviction / residency AND context management / masking / truncation / pruning / hit rate): 15 all-time, 14 in the 12-month window; Q2 (prefix cache AND rollout AND RL AND agent): 2 all-time. On target and fetched: 2610.22863 (trace replay of LRU under budgets, production M365 traces, Llama-2-70B KV layout stand-in; no context-policy arm; residency as a fleet question), 2608.11152 MISA-T (residency-time-aware admission for mixed RL rollouts on Step3.7 and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, +43.6-53.3% rollout throughput 'while maintaining high prefix-cache hit rates', i.e. it stays below the cliff by admission and never asks what a context policy does to the cliff), 2610.36355 WAKMan (eviction-policy choice by workload mix; agentic steps favor recency), 2606.01065 Leyline and 2605.27744 / 2608.14624 CacheScout (serving-side primitives and agent-aware eviction; no context-policy comparison), 2507.07400 KVFlow (workflow-aware eviction, 'up to 2.19x speedup for scenarios with many concurrent workflows'; fixed agent prompts, not growing histories). Occupied by the card: the single-tenant executed-prefill accounting and the break-even formula. Occupied by CADOC / TokenPilot / TurnCost (W43 kill record): the priced break-even under stable caching and the re-scoring of public trajectories with a uniform cache-efficiency factor, which cannot produce a cliff. Not occupied: the interaction of context policy with residency regime on a real engine, the crossover concurrency, and the regime label on published rollout configurations. Kill-search vocabulary (the neighbours' words, per the W43 lesson): stack distance, working set, thrash, cache pressure, residency, admission, sessions per GPU, closed-loop, hit rate versus concurrency, rollout concurrency, cache-aware router, time-to-live.
scorecard.why_now: Card 2026-10-26 (physical accounting, $\rho$ left at ceiling); 2610.22863 2026-10-16 (residency replay under budgets); MISA-T 2026-08-11 (residency-aware rollout admission); WAKMan 2026-10-26 (agentic recency); FlashNext-RL 2026-10-20 (a published rollout configuration to grade). The law is from 1970; the flag is recorded.
scorecard.register_and_not: Measurement with a one-line law and a recipe consequence (which context default in which regime; how many sessions per GPU). It is not a new eviction policy (KVFlow, CacheScout, WAKMan), not an admission scheduler (MISA-T), not a context-management method (CADOC, TokenPilot, AKV); the edit-on-miss arm is a bound on cache-aware editing, not a proposal; and it is not a quality study, since the trajectories are fixed and the card's quality gate (26 vs 29 of 100, failed at $\epsilon = 5$ for lack of power, card weakest_component (5)) is left as it stands.

identifiability: Random given: the recorded trajectory set (fixed text, so no model decision and no sampling temperature enters), the serialization operator, the engine and its block size and eviction rule (LRU), the KV budget $B$, the session count $N$, the wait $W$ and the seeded arrival order; residual variation is scheduler timing jitter under concurrency, reported over two orderings. Decode content is discarded and only its recorded length is reproduced, so residency time per call matches the original run and nothing depends on which model generated the text; tokenizer mismatch between the recording model and the served model changes counts by a few percent and is reported. The hit fraction is therefore a property of (policy, protocol), which is the Gate 0 point: the card's +608.5% is the protocol's value at $N = 1$, $W$ = sandbox latency, $B$ = 128 GB unified memory, and the paper's own formula says it is not a property of masking. The stack-distance law assumes symmetric sessions in a cycle; heterogeneous and growing working sets smear the cliff, which the step-0 simulation predicts exactly and the replay checks.
positioning_note: Lab-adjacent: a measurement on open engines with public trajectories that grades published systems configurations (FlashNext-RL, MISA-T) without competing with them; the systems labs that own the schedulers are consumers, not rivals. Solo covers step 0 and step 1 on one rented H100 or the DGX Spark. Lab adds the live version: the rollout engine's hit counters over an RL run, which is import S6xF7's pass B. title: Drift or diffusion: the growth law of the prefix log-ratio separates arithmetic mismatch from cache-eviction mismatch
statement: On teacher-forced replays of recorded agent trajectories, compute per policy token $\delta_t := \log q_{\mathrm{text}}(x_t \mid \tilde{h}_t) - \log r_{\mathrm{exec}}(x_t \mid \mathcal{C}_t)$ (the trainer's recompute from the text it sees, $\tilde{h}_t$, minus the engine's own log-probability of the token it sampled from its state $\mathcal{C}_t$) under two mismatch sources on the same model and the same trajectories: arithmetic (the card paper's stack, vLLM FP8 W8A8 plus per-token FP8 KV cache with the full cache, against a BF16 HF forward on the same text; and BF16 engine against BF16 HF as the floor) and conditioning (the AKV engine's served state after drop and repos against contiguous re-prefill of the retained text, both BF16). Remove the Gibbs drift from the prefix sum, $M_n := E_n - n\,\bar{\delta}$ with $E_n := \sum_{u \le n} \delta_u$, $n$ the number of policy tokens since the episode start (arithmetic arm) or since the last drop (eviction arm), and $\bar{\delta}$ the arm mean, and fit the growth exponent $H$ in $\mathrm{Var}[M_n] \propto n^{2H}$ across trajectories at fixed $n$. Also report the fraction of tokens whose raw $E_n$ lies outside InterQ-RL's envelope $[-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}} \sqrt{n}, \epsilon_{\mathrm{high}} \sqrt{n}]$ (eq. 5, $\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}} = 0.025$, $\epsilon_{\mathrm{high}} = 0.05$) in each arm.
claim: Rollout-trainer mismatch from arithmetic and mismatch from KV-cache eviction have different growth laws: once the Gibbs drift is removed, the arithmetic prefix log-ratio spreads as $\sqrt{n}$ (diffusive, $H \approx 1/2$) while the post-eviction prefix log-ratio grows as $n$ (ballistic, $H \to 1$), so the exponent read from the log-probabilities a trainer already stores says which mismatch a run has, and a $\sqrt{n}$ envelope sized for the first truncates the second.
trick: Add up, token by token, how much the trainer and the engine disagree about the words the agent wrote: rounding noise piles up like a random walk, a missing piece of context pushes every later token the same way, and the slope of the pile-up tells the two apart.
why_now: InterQ-RL (2610.35303, October 2026) writes the rollout-learner ratio as a history factor times a current-token factor (card, eq. 3-4) and bounds the history factor with the $\sqrt{n_t}$ envelope it borrows from CTPO (2605.07331, May 2026), whose abstract states the design assumption in its own words: clip bounds scale 'according to the natural $\sqrt{t}$ growth of the cumulative log-ratio'. AKV (2610.28577, October 2026) ships an engine that teacher-forces any cache-operation history in one prefill, so the eviction arm is a configuration, not a kernel. The identity behind the drift, $\mathbb{E}_{x_t \sim r_{\mathrm{exec}}}[\delta_t] = -D_{\mathrm{KL}}(r_{\mathrm{exec}} \,\|\, q_{\mathrm{text}})$ (Gibbs' inequality; the card's eq. 11 is its estimator), is textbook, and the flag is recorded that nothing in the readout is new beyond the pairing.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 (zero GPU, one day, written before any run): with $\mathbb{E}[\delta_t] = -\mathrm{KL}$ per token, the expected raw prefix sum after $n$ tokens is $-n \cdot \mathrm{KL}$ and crosses InterQ-RL's lower envelope $-\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}} \sqrt{n}$ at $n^{*} = (\epsilon_{\mathrm{low}} / \mathrm{KL})^{2}$; with the card's K3 anchors (sec. 3.1, median over the final 20 steps) this gives $n^{*} < 1$ token at the aligned-quantized level ($\mathrm{KL} \approx 0.029$) and $n^{*} \approx 319$ tokens at the BF16 level ($\mathrm{KL} \approx 0.0014$). Prediction: in the paper's own regime the lower clip binds in expectation from the first policy token and the history weight reduces to $\overline{W}_t = \exp(-0.025 \sqrt{n_t})$, a depth discount. Step 1 (about 30 GPU-h, 5 days): 60 trajectories of Qwen3-8B (the card paper's ScienceWorld model; GPT-OSS-20B if the AKV fork serves only that family, in which case the arithmetic arm runs on the same model in vLLM BF16 versus FP8-KV only) on SWE-bench Verified with mini-SWE-agent under AKV's drop-all-but-the-latest-12 tool responses with repos, temperature 1.0 as in the paper, operation sequence and engine log-probs logged (reuse C-W43-25's 90 recorded trajectories if they exist). Five teacher-forced passes per trajectory: vLLM FP8 W8A8 plus FP8 E4M3 per-token KV on the full text (the paper's rollout config, App. C.1), vLLM BF16 on the full text, HF BF16 on the full text, AKV served state under the recorded operations, AKV contiguous re-prefill of the retained text. Form $\delta^{N}_t$ (FP8 engine minus HF), $\delta^{0}_t$ (BF16 engine minus HF) and $\delta^{E}_t$ (served state minus text state); per arm compute $\bar{\delta}$, $M_n$, $\mathrm{Var}[M_n]$ across trajectories at $n \in \{8, 16, 32, \ldots, 1024\}$ (clock reset at each drop in the eviction arm), the least-squares slope $2H$ on log-log axes with a bootstrap band over trajectories, the lag-$k$ autocorrelation of $\delta_t$ for $k \le 64$ (the mechanism: $H > 1/2$ is positively correlated increments), the envelope-exceedance fraction, and $\bar{\delta}$ in K3 units against the paper's three anchors (1.03 unaligned, 0.029 aligned, 0.0014 BF16).
killing_experiment.kills_if: The fitted exponents $H^{E}$ (post-drop) and $H^{N}$ (arithmetic, same model) agree within 0.1 with overlapping bootstrap bands, on the centred sums: eviction mismatch accumulates like arithmetic mismatch, the exponent does not discriminate, and a $\sqrt{n}$-envelope correction fed by log-probabilities alone (InterQ-RL, CTPO) covers the eviction term too, which withdraws the 'log the operation sequence' consequence of CL-W43-11 and leaves the claim its ghost-information half (C-W43-24). That negative is citable on its own. Established if $H^{E} \geq H^{N} + 0.25$ with disjoint bands. Separately, step 0's prediction is refuted if fewer than half of the arithmetic-arm tokens at $n > 50$ sit on the lower envelope boundary, in which case the clip is a correction as the paper says and the depth-discount reading is dropped.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.55: $H^{N} \in [0.5, 0.65]$ after centring (rounding errors weakly correlated; the FP8 KV write persists, so some memory), $H^{E} \in [0.8, 1.0]$ over the first 200 policy tokens after a drop and decaying toward 0.5 as the dropped content stops mattering; the arithmetic arm's raw $E_n$ sits on the lower envelope for more than 80% of tokens past $n = 50$. Probability 0.25: both exponents near 1 (persistent FP8 KV error makes arithmetic mismatch ballistic too), the ruler is dead and the $\sqrt{n}$ envelope is wrong for both. Probability 0.20: both near 0.5, the probe kills.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: CTPO's abstract: 'position-adaptive clipping that scales log-space clip bounds according to the natural $\sqrt{t}$ growth of the cumulative log-ratio'. InterQ-RL, sec. 3.2 (card): rollout-learner discrepancies are 'two evaluations of the same checkpoint along different numerical paths', so all mismatch is arithmetic and the envelope $\pm 0.05 \sqrt{n_t}$ is a correction rather than a truncation (the card's load-bearing assumption). The same paper admits it has no scalar that says when history-level correction is needed: 'A low K3 alone does not imply strong task performance' (sec. 4.2).
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: If the exponents separate: a trainer detects conditioning mismatch (eviction, compaction, cache edits) from the log-probabilities it already stores, with no operation log, and every $\sqrt{n}$-envelope correction must switch off or grow its envelope linearly after a drop. If they do not: the eviction term is absorbed by shipped history-level corrections and CL-W43-11 asks nothing of trainers beyond what InterQ-RL already does. If step 0's prediction holds in the arithmetic arm: InterQ-RL's history weight is a depth discount in its own regime, and its +6.0 over QAT on ALFWorld (sec. 4.2) is the effect of down-weighting late actions, a re-reading that the paper's collapsing 'Prefix' and 'Global' variants (App. C.4) do not exclude.

scorecard.target_value: In print: CTPO's '$\sqrt{t}$ growth' design assumption; InterQ-RL's envelope sized for an arithmetic residual and its sec. 4.2 admission that K3 does not say when history-level correction is needed; the Zero-Mismatch Reference (2605.14220): 'TIM is not benign numerical noise, but a systems-level perturbation that should be treated as a first-order factor'. Who pays: training teams choosing a correction for quantized or evicting rollouts (verl users of the FP8-RL stack); serving teams asked whether the operation log must ship with every trajectory; the authors of the $\sqrt{t}$ envelope.

impact_ceiling.floor: A note with the identity, the boundary-hit fraction on InterQ-RL's own stack (the depth-discount re-reading) and the exponent on one model; requires step 0 and the arithmetic arm; judgment p 0.45.
impact_ceiling.middle: The exponents separate on one model and the two-number diagnostic ($\bar{\delta}$ and $H$) is adopted by one open agentic-RL stack as a mismatch monitor beside K3; requires step 1; judgment p 0.35.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The exponent predicts which recompute path holds training (text versus operation-aware, the ceiling run of the companion gradient probe) on two models, and the envelope rule is rewritten in CTPO's and InterQ-RL's successors; requires a training comparison of about 150 GPU-h from a lab position; judgment p 0.15.

title: Does the eviction term reach the gradient: text recompute, InterQ-RL weights and operation-aware recompute on the same rollouts
statement: Take two batches $\mathcal{B}$, $\mathcal{B}'$ of 64 agent rollouts each (8 prompts times 8 responses, GRPO group-normalized advantages from official test rewards), sampled under KV-cache eviction on the AKV engine (drop all but the latest 12 tool responses, then repos) with Qwen3-8B on SWE-bench Verified, the operation sequence and the engine's per-token log-probabilities logged. At the sampling checkpoint compute the policy gradient three ways from the same rollouts and rewards: $g_{\mathrm{text}}$ (the trainer recomputes from the retained text prefilled contiguously, today's practice), $g_{\mathrm{IQ}}$ (the same, with InterQ-RL's history weights $W_t$ from eqs. 5-9 computed from the engine's logged log-probabilities and the text recompute), and $g_{\mathrm{op}}$ (the trainer reproduces the engine's conditioning with a block attention mask and the repositioned position ids, so each token attends to exactly what the engine attended to; the trainer-side twin of AKV's segment-batch attention). Measure the bias $\|g_{\mathrm{text}} - g_{\mathrm{op}}\|$ and $\|g_{\mathrm{IQ}} - g_{\mathrm{op}}\|$ against the batch's own sampling noise $\sigma := \|g_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathcal{B}) - g_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathcal{B}')\| / \sqrt{2}$, the cosine between the two batches' bias vectors, and the same ratio at sub-batch sizes 16 and 32.
claim: At the batch sizes agentic GRPO trains with, recomputing log-probabilities from the text of rollouts that were served under KV eviction biases the policy gradient by an amount comparable to the batch's sampling noise and in a direction that repeats across batches, and the history-level correction that fixes quantization mismatch removes less than a third of it because it is sized for a diffusing, not a drifting, log-ratio.
trick: Compute the training update three ways from the same episodes: pretending the text is what the model saw, applying the quantization paper's fix, and rebuilding exactly what the model saw; then ask whether the pretend update differs from the exact one by more than the dice do.
why_now: AKV (2610.28577, October 2026) ships an engine that logs the operation sequence and reconstructs any operation history in one prefill, which is the specification for the trainer-side mask in $g_{\mathrm{op}}$; InterQ-RL (2610.35303, October 2026) gives a history-level weight computable from log-probabilities alone, so the question 'does a shipped correction absorb the eviction term' can be asked without training; the Zero-Mismatch Reference (2605.14220, May 2026) shows that 'small token-level numerical disagreements can independently cause training collapse', which makes the size of a larger, structured term at the gradient a live question; import:2026-W43-S6xF7 predicts KV residency binds agentic-RL throughput, so eviction inside rollouts is the next lever systems teams ship.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 (about 5 GPU-h, 3 days of engineering): implement the operation-aware recompute as one HF forward with a 4-D attention mask (tokens generated before a drop attend to the dropped tool response; tokens after it do not) and position ids that follow the repos; validate it by checking that its token log-probabilities match the engine's logged values at the BF16 floor (K3 at the 0.0014 level, card sec. 3.1) and that, before the first drop in every episode, $g_{\mathrm{text}}$ and $g_{\mathrm{op}}$ agree to the batch-arithmetic floor (a built-in null; if it fails, the reproduction is wrong and the probe stops). Step 1 (about 55 GPU-h, 6 days): sample the two batches (about 40 GPU-h on 2 H100-class GPUs, episodes capped at 100 steps with the effective context set so that drops fire in most episodes), then compute the three gradients per batch with backprop over all parameters and no optimizer step (gradient at $\theta = \theta_{\mathrm{old}}$, so PPO clipping is inactive and $g = \sum_{\tau} \sum_{t} A_{\tau} m_t \nabla_{\theta} \log q_{\theta}(x_t \mid \cdot)$ with $A_{\tau}$ the group-normalized advantage and $m_t$ the policy-token mask), repeating $g_{\mathrm{op}}$ once to record the batch-arithmetic floor. Readouts: $\beta_{\mathrm{text}} := \|g_{\mathrm{text}} - g_{\mathrm{op}}\| / \sigma$ and $\beta_{\mathrm{IQ}}$ likewise; the cross-batch cosine $c$ between $g_{\mathrm{text}}(\mathcal{B}) - g_{\mathrm{op}}(\mathcal{B})$ and the same vector on $\mathcal{B}'$; the removal fraction $1 - \beta_{\mathrm{IQ}} / \beta_{\mathrm{text}}$; all three per layer and split by tokens before versus after the first drop; $\beta_{\mathrm{text}}$ at sub-batch sizes 16, 32, 64, since $\sigma$ falls as $1/\sqrt{N}$ and a bias does not.
killing_experiment.kills_if: $\beta_{\mathrm{text}} < 0.25$ and $|c| < 0.2$ on both batches at $N = 64$: the eviction term does not reach the gradient at training batch sizes, text recompute is adequate under this drop policy, and CL-W43-11's trainer half is a per-token curiosity with no training consequence (citable as: cache eviction inside rollouts needs no trainer change at $K = 12$). Established if $\beta_{\mathrm{text}} \geq 0.5$ and $c \geq 0.5$. The InterQ-RL arm is read separately: a removal fraction above $2/3$ means a shipped log-probability-only correction suffices and the operation log is unnecessary; below $1/3$ it does not.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.50: $\beta_{\mathrm{text}} \in [0.5, 1.5]$ at $N = 64$, rising with $N$, $c > 0.5$, and InterQ-RL's weights remove under a third of the bias (its raw prefix sum sits on the lower clip, so the weight is a depth discount that carries no information about the drop's direction). Probability 0.30: the bias is small and unstructured, the probe kills. Probability 0.20: the bias is large and InterQ-RL's weights remove most of it, so log-probabilities suffice and the operation log is not needed.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: InterQ-RL, sec. 3.2 (card): the rollout-learner discrepancy is 'two evaluations of the same checkpoint along different numerical paths', and the trainer's input is 'all turns of an episode ... as one concatenated sequence' (App. C.1). AKV names 'training agents under this scheme' as future work (sec. 6, per card 2610.28577). The Zero-Mismatch Reference: mismatch 'should be treated as a first-order factor in analyzing LLM RL stability', measured for the arithmetic case only. Agentic-RL stacks record token sequences as the trajectory (C-W43-25's stated assumption, to be verified against their code at the kill search).
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: Established: the trajectory record for evicting rollouts must carry the operation sequence, or trainers must forbid eviction; shipped log-probability corrections do not substitute; this is the gradient-level consequence CL-W43-11 needs before any training comparison. Killed: cache eviction is a free serving lever inside RL at this drop policy, which unblocks CL-W43-12's KV-residency lever without a trainer change, and no InterQ-RL-style correction is needed for eviction either. Bias large but removed by InterQ-RL's weights: the operation log is unnecessary and the claim's consequence shrinks to 'use a history-level weight', which changes what CL-W43-11 asks of trainers.

scorecard.target_value: In print: AKV's future-work sentence on training under cache operations; InterQ-RL's admission that no scalar says when history-level correction is needed (sec. 4.2); the Zero-Mismatch Reference's 'first-order factor'. Who pays: agentic-RL infrastructure teams (verl, SkyRL, prime-rl and the others named in import S6xF7) deciding whether eviction is allowed inside rollouts; serving-engine teams deciding whether to expose the operation log; users of the FP8-RL stack who would otherwise reach for InterQ-RL's weights.

impact_ceiling.floor: A null with numbers: eviction at K = 12 does not move the gradient beyond noise; cited by anyone shipping eviction inside rollouts; requires step 1; judgment p 0.30.
impact_ceiling.middle: A structured bias comparable to the sampling noise, a batch-size curve, and the trainer-side operation-aware recompute (one HF forward with a block mask) as the shipped artifact, adopted by one open stack; requires step 1; judgment p 0.45.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The training comparison (KV-drop rollouts with text recompute, with operation-aware recompute, and TEXT-drop rollouts with exact recompute, about 150 GPU-h, lab position) shows the biased arm regressing late as InterQ-RL's alignment-only arm did (95.5% to 89.6% between steps 300 and 400, sec. 4.2); operation logs become a standard field of agentic-RL trajectory records; judgment p 0.25.

relevance.jacobs_edge: Direct: bias against noise of a vector estimator, an identity-level question (same advantages, different conditioning); the mask reproduction is GPU engineering. No physics content.

scorecard.kill_probe: 128 rollouts under eviction, three recompute paths with backprop, one 8B model, about 60 GPU-h, about $220, 9 days; dead if the bias is under a quarter of the sampling noise and unstructured on both batches.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: From the card's fetched neighbours: FP8-RL 2601.18150, AIS 2605.13907 and Jet-RL 2601.14243 measure K3-type per-token divergences and never a gradient bias; the Zero-Mismatch Reference 2605.14220 isolates arithmetic mismatch by an exact rollout path and is the control-arm shape this probe copies into the conditioning case; CTPO 2605.07331 corrects policy-version drift. Nothing in the card's neighbours computes a conditioning-aware gradient. Owned: InterQ-RL's weight (eqs. 5-9); AKV's segment-batch attention (the engine-side version of the mask). Spot-check on the day of writing (arXiv API, 2026-11-01): abs 'training-inference mismatch' AND 'KV cache' 5 entries, none on eviction; abs 'importance' AND 'rollout' AND 'eviction' 0. Kill-search words: training-inference mismatch, off-policy correction, importance sampling, rollout engine, KV cache eviction, attention mask, gradient bias, policy-gradient variance.

scorecard.register_and_not: A controlled comparison in the measurement register (three recompute paths on the same rollouts) with a recipe consequence (log operations, forbid eviction, or trust a shipped weight). Not a new correction, not a training run, not a serving engine, not the card's method on another benchmark.

identifiability: The three arms share rollouts and rewards, so the advantages $A_{\tau}$ are identical and the only difference is the conditioning of $q_{\theta}$; the sampling noise is estimated from an independent batch under the identical protocol and the batch-arithmetic noise from a repeated $g_{\mathrm{op}}$. SWE-bench is deterministic after the action, so the only randomness at generation is the policy's sampling at temperature 1.0, held fixed. Batch size is a protocol constant and is the point: the bias-to-noise ratio is reported as a curve over $N \in \{16, 32, 64\}$, never as one number. The pre-first-drop split is the built-in null that certifies the reproduction. No judge or critic enters; the reward is the official test verifier.
positioning_note: Lab-adjacent systems measurement under one GPU-week on open weights, a released engine and an HF forward; solo is sufficient for step 1. A lab training agents under eviction runs it on its own batches in a day; the ceiling (two to three training arms) is the lab-position version and is not the probe. Dropped operators: 1 (replacing InterQ-RL's envelope with a drift-aware one is a new correction, lab-contested and solo-killed under L2's out-of-scope rule); 2 (the trainer moved to where the operation information exists is the reference arm, not the candidate).

title: Where message-attributable handoff failures sit: dropped, in view and unused, or followed from an invented entry — the census with its full-history pair
statement: On HSC-Bench's continuation track (739 tasks x 6 receivers; the sheet, transcript-tail and full-history arms are already run for all six, Table 2; the authors' outputs are requested first) and on Compact-Bench's public paired full-history / summary-only continuations (2610.31710) as the corpus that needs no email, take every criterion a receiver fails under the handoff message and passes under full history, and label it with the benchmark's own typed matcher: the needed value was dropped (in the source history, not in the message), corrupted (a different sourced value in its field), in view and unused (in the message, sourced, and still not reported), or followed from an unsourced entry (the receiver's reported value equals a message entry that matches nothing in the source history); criteria failed under both arms are the receiver's baseline and are reported beside the cells. A placebo message from another task of the same scenario family gives the chance-match rate of every cell, intervals are bootstrapped over scenario families, and the unsourced-entry share of every message is published first so the followed-unsourced cell is read against its base rate. The repository track (300 ContextBench-annotated tasks on public CodeTraceBench GPT-5 trajectories) is the fallback if no continuation data are shared: there the typed values are file paths, the oracle is the gold annotation, and the full-history arm is ours to run.
claim: Fewer than one in ten message-attributable handoff failures — a criterion failed under the 1,600-character sheet and passed under full history by the same receiver — are the receiver acting on an entry the writer invented; the remainder are a needed value the sheet dropped or a value in view that the receiver did not use.
trick: Pair each handoff failure with the same receiver's full-history run, keep only the failures the message caused, and sort them by whether the needed fact was dropped, left unused, or replaced by something the writer made up.
why_now: HSC-Bench (2026-10-27) ran the full-history arm for all six receivers on 739 typed-criterion tasks (sec. 4.1, Table 2) and never computed per-entry provenance; Compact-Bench (2026-10-22) released paired full-history / summary-only continuations with code and data; the C-W43-23 red team (2026-10-25) wrote down the uncompressed control and the typed matcher this census needs and found both absent on AppWorld. The three pieces landed within two weeks; the flag is that the lane produced about eight compaction papers in the same two weeks.

killing_experiment.kills_if: For at least three of six receivers the family-clustered 95% lower bound of $\pi_{\mathrm{inv}}$ among message-attributable failures is above 0.10 and above the placebo chance-match rate: the writer's invented entries are a main cause of handoff failure, CL-W43-05's mechanism carries from iterative compaction to one-shot handoff sheets, and this census is its second benchmark. An interval straddling 0.10 is reported as such and settles nothing. Protocol kill: if more than 25% of message-attributable failures are unclassifiable under the typed matcher (composed or derived values), the probe parks with that number.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.6: $\pi_{\mathrm{inv}} < 0.10$ for every receiver, with unsourced entries under 15% of sheet entries and concentrated in remaining-work fields; in-view-unused is the largest cell (0.4-0.6) on tool and file-work tasks and dropped the largest on conversational tasks; the placebo chance-match rate is under 0.05 under typed matching.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: CL-W43-05's current belief, from SJC 2610.20927: 25 of 35 analysed compaction failures (71%) follow a summary entry no environment output supports or that contradicts one. The card's paper assumes the opposite without a count: 'The failure occurs after the necessary completion information has reached the receiver' (sec. 5.4) and 'these results highlight the importance of how the receiver uses the supplied information to determine what to do next' (sec. 5.5), resting on 2 repeats of 114 continuations.
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: If following an invented entry is under a tenth of message-caused failures, the provenance gate is the wrong first lever for handoff messages and the lane's ruler needs a use axis (in view and unused) that no published handoff or compaction score has. If it is above a quarter, unsourced persistence is a property of LLM-written state regardless of write regime, and SJC's gate belongs in every handoff writer.

identifiability: Random given: the task, the recorded source history, the fixed messages (one GPT-4.1 sheet and one transcript tail per task), temperature 0 and top-$p$ 1 at each receiver (App. A), so the (sheet, full) pair differs only in the message and provider nondeterminism; the cells are properties of the (writer, receiver, benchmark) triple and are reported as such, never as 'handoffs' in general. The matcher is the benchmark's own criterion rule typed by field, so a bare integer in the wrong field does not match, and chance membership is measured by the placebo, not assumed. The reference-leak rule (the receiver supplies the reference when the history has none) is excluded by construction. No judge: the 150-label audit checks the matcher, not a labeler. Full history is the control that C-W43-23 lacked: under it every value is in view, so 'dropped' is zero by construction and the paired difference isolates the message.

title: The provenance gate, judge-free, on a one-shot handoff sheet: delete the unsourced entries at matched tokens
statement: On HSC-Bench's continuation track (authors' tasks) and on the rebuilt repository track, add two arms to the existing transcript-tail / sheet / full-history triple at the same visible token count: sourced-only state (the GPT-4.1 sheet with every entry whose typed value matches nothing in the pre-handoff history deleted, whitespace-padded to the original token count, the paper's own device in App. A) and extractive-matched (verbatim history lines that carry the sheet's sourced typed values, selected greedily by criterion-field coverage up to the same token count). Score all-criteria pass rate and mean score per receiver with paired scenario-family bootstrap against the sheet, report the unsourced-entry share of each sheet and the deleted-entry count per message, and the per-criterion deltas in Table 5's format. The matched quantities are the visible token count and the set of sourced typed values; the matcher and the unsourced list come from the census candidate in this file.
claim: Deleting every unsourced entry from a one-shot handoff sheet — the Source-Judged Compaction gate run with a typed matcher instead of a judge — changes each receiver's all-criteria pass rate by under 2 points: the gate that earns +5.3 accuracy on iterative compaction summaries is inert on sheets written once from the whole history.
trick: Run the compaction paper's delete-the-unsourced-bullets rule on a handoff sheet with a string matcher instead of a judge, and see whether the receiver scores any differently.
why_now: SJC's gate (2026-10-14) is the only published intervention on unsourced entries and was run in one regime (iterative, 4,096-token window, AppWorld, one agent model); HSC-Bench (2026-10-27) supplies the one-shot regime with six receivers, typed criteria and a full-history ceiling at matched tokens; the typed matcher the C-W43-23 red team specified (2026-10-25) replaces SJC's judge, so the gate becomes judge-free and the arm costs one API pass.

killing_experiment.design: Prerequisite: the census candidate's step 1 labeler (unsourced entries per sheet, $U_i$). Power gate, pre-registered: if unsourced entries are under 10% of sheet entries on a track, the deletion arm on that track is reported as underpowered and the track contributes its entry census only. Arms: sourced-only state $S_i \setminus U_i$ padded to the sheet's visible token count; extractive-matched $E_i$, the verbatim history lines containing the typed values of $S_i \cap H_i$, added greedily by number of criterion fields covered until the token count is reached; plus the three existing arms. Volume: 739 x 6 x 2 = 8,868 continuations on HSC (about 3K input and 1K output tokens each, $150-250 at list prices across six providers) or 300 x 6 x 2 = 3,600 single-call predictions on the rebuilt repository track (under $50). Readouts, with $\hat p$ the all-criteria pass rate and subscripts $R$, $S$, $D$, $E$ for transcript tail, sheet, sourced-only sheet and extractive arm: $\Delta_D = \hat p_D - \hat p_S$ (the gate's effect), the recovered share $g = (\hat p_E - \hat p_R)/(\hat p_S - \hat p_R)$ (how much of the sheet's gain is selection), each with paired family-cluster 95% intervals; the same on mean score and on line-F1; per-criterion deltas so that a sign flip of the kind in Table 4 (+ status match) is visible by field rather than hidden in the aggregate.
killing_experiment.kills_if: For at least three of six receivers the family-clustered 95% interval of $\Delta_D$ excludes zero and $|\Delta_D| \geq 2$ points: positive, the gate helps on one-shot sheets, CL-W43-05's lever transfers and SJC's +5.3 has a judge-free replication; negative, the unsourced entries (the writer's plans and inferences) carry value and delete-by-default is the wrong design. Underpowered (unsourced share under 10%) is reported as a census, not as a kill, and hands the question to the write-regime candidate.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.55: $|\Delta_D| < 2$ points for every receiver with unsourced entries at 5-15% of sheet entries, concentrated in remaining-work fields; $g \geq 0.8$ on tool and conversational tasks and under 0.5 on file-work tasks, where the sheet alone was given the output field names (sec. 4.1).
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: SJC: deleting unsourced entries raises AppWorld accuracy by 5.3 and Pass3 by 8.9 points (per the C-W43-08 and C-W43-23 records); CL-W43-05's if_true: 'Compactors label or delete unsourced entries by default'; the card's paper attributes the sheet's advantage to 'the information selected and its presentation together' (sec. 5.5) and separates neither from provenance.
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: An inert gate means provenance is a correlate of the iterative regime, not of LLM-written state, and compaction evaluations should add retention and use axes before a provenance axis. An effect of at least 2 points either way is the first judge-free, receiver-paired measurement of what unsourced entries do, with its sign, and a positive sign gives CL-W43-05 its second benchmark.

identifiability: As the census candidate, plus: whitespace padding holds the visible token count fixed (App. A), so the deletion arm differs from the sheet only in the deleted entries; the deleted set is defined by the typed matcher and is reproducible from the message and the history alone; the extractive arm's selection rule is fixed and published; all receivers at temperature 0 and top-$p$ 1; effects are per (writer, receiver, benchmark). The gate is SJC's in rule but not in judge: a judge-free twin, which is the point, and the difference is stated wherever the +5.3 is compared.
positioning_note: Solo feasible on the rebuilt repository track; the continuation track needs the authors (lab or email). Dropped: the narrative-summary arm (GPT-5.4 only; 284 of 739 truncated; the paper's own confound, Table 8) is not re-run; operator 3 (chained handoffs) as in the census candidate.

Who pays: compactor builders deciding whether to ship a provenance gate; harness teams writing orchestrator briefs; compaction evaluators.

impact_ceiling.middle: The gate's effect shown to be regime-dependent (inert one-shot, positive iterative at matched budget) and CL-W43-05 rewritten to name the regime. Requires the write-regime candidate as well. Judgment p 0.3.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: A published rule, provenance gates for iterative compactors and retention for one-shot writers, adopted by one product harness. Requires a second writer and a production corpus. Judgment p 0.1.

title: Unsourced entries by write regime: the same writer and budget, iterating on its own summary versus rewriting from the raw log
statement: On the rebuilt HSC repository track (300 public CodeTraceBench GPT-5 histories, ten action-observation pairs each) and on SJC's AppWorld harness (147 train+dev tasks x 3 runs, 4,096-token window, the only split with reference solutions), produce at every boundary two messages at the same character budget from the same writer and prompt: iterative (the writer sees its previous summary plus the steps since, as compaction does) and one-shot (the writer sees the whole raw history to that point, as the card's handoff writer does). Label every entry sourced or unsourced with the typed matcher against the raw history, and report the unsourced-entry share per message by regime and boundary index, the retention of later-needed typed values (annotated paths; AppWorld needed values from the reference solutions' state-changing calls), and the receiver's score under each message (line-F1; AppWorld accuracy and Pass3). The matched quantities are the writer, the prompt, the budget and the boundary.
claim: Unsourced entries in compaction summaries are made by iterating on a prior summary: at the same budget and boundary, the same writer rewriting from the raw log produces fewer than half as many entries that match nothing in the history.
trick: Compact the same trajectory twice, once by updating the old summary and once from scratch off the raw log, and count which one invents more.
why_now: SJC (2026-10-14) counted unsourced entries only in the iterative regime (13-21% of entries pruned, Open TODOs 67.7% unsourced, per the C-W43-08 record); the card's paper (2026-10-27) ran only the one-shot regime and never counted; 'Benchmarks Are Surprisingly Compaction-Friendly' (2610.31778, 2026-10-22) measured the omission side of the regime effect, dropped constraints rising 'monotonically with the number of compactions', and the commission side is unmeasured. The raw log is always on disk, so the one-shot arm is a free recipe if the count favours it.

killing_experiment.design: Repository track: for each of 300 histories, boundaries after steps 2, 4, 6, 8 and 10. Iterative arm: GPT-4.1 given (previous sheet, steps since the last boundary) writes a 1,800-character sheet; one-shot arm: GPT-4.1 given all steps to the boundary writes a 1,800-character sheet; same prompt otherwise (ours, published). 1,500 writer calls per arm, about 9M tokens each, about $25 per arm. Typed matcher on paths, symbols, line numbers and command strings against the raw history gives $u_{b}^{(\mathrm{iter})}$ and $u_{b}^{(\mathrm{one})}$, the unsourced share of entries at boundary $b$. Receivers: six at the step-10 boundary under each sheet (300 x 6 x 2 single calls, under $40), scored by line-F1 against ContextBench gold; retention of annotated paths per arm (the paper's $\rho$, sec. 5.3). AppWorld: SJC's harness with a second compaction method, raw-rewrite (one-shot from the full logged trajectory at each harness-triggered boundary, same OpenClaw prompt and budget), against the stock iterative compressor; 147 tasks x 3 runs per arm at 112.8K tokens per task, $110-150 per arm at GPT-5.6 Luna list price (C-W43-23 red team's figure); the iterative arm is free if SJC's authors share Prompting-arm logs. Readouts: $\bar u$ per regime with boundary-indexed curves, the ratio $\rho_u = \bar u^{(\mathrm{iter})} / \bar u^{(\mathrm{one})}$ with family (repository) or scenario (AppWorld) cluster bootstrap, the split of unsourced entries into identifiers versus plans to compare with SJC's Table 2, retention of later-needed values per arm, and receiver scores per arm.
killing_experiment.kills_if: The cluster-bootstrapped 95% upper bound of $\rho_u$ is below 2 on both corpora: iterating on a prior summary does not multiply unsourced entries, the writer invents at the same rate from the raw log, and the provenance gate rather than re-compaction from raw is the lever, a citable negative for every harness that keeps the raw log. A second kill: if the one-shot arm retains later-needed values at a rate more than 10 points below the iterative arm at the same budget, the regime comparison is confounded by what each arm keeps and is parked with that number.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.5: $\rho_u$ between 2 and 4 on AppWorld, driven by plan sections (Open TODOs, pending asks), near 1 for exact identifiers; under 1.5 on the repository track, where paths are copied rather than inferred; receiver scores equal within noise on both.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: SJC treats unsourced entries as a property of the summary to be gated entry by entry ('Prune the Summary, Not the History'); CL-W43-05's if_true is 'compactors label or delete unsourced entries by default'; the card's writer is one-shot and its paper never asks the question; the recursive-memory line (Wang et al. 2308.15022: 'recursively produce new memory using previous memory and following contexts') reports consistency gains and no invention count.
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: If $\rho_u \geq 2$, the cheapest compaction fix is to rewrite from the raw log instead of the prior summary, and CL-W43-05's mechanism is re-scoped to the iterative regime with its if_true changed from 'delete' to 'rewrite'. If $\rho_u < 2$, invention is the writer's and regime-independent, and SJC's gate is the lever in every regime.

identifiability: Random given: the recorded history, the writer (GPT-4.1 or the SJC compressor model) at temperature 0, the prompt and the budget; the two arms differ only in the writer's input (prior summary plus delta versus raw log). Unsourced is defined against the raw history, which both arms could in principle see, so a one-shot entry is unsourced only by invention while an iterative entry is unsourced by invention or by inheriting an earlier invention; $\rho_u$ measures inheritance plus any regime-induced invention, and the boundary-indexed curve separates them (inheritance grows with $b$, fresh invention does not). On the repository track the source history is fixed, so arms are paired at every boundary; on AppWorld the agent acts on the summary after the first boundary, so arms are paired at the first boundary and marginal after, and the record says which number is which. Retention is measured so that a regime that invents less by keeping less is caught by the second kill.
positioning_note: The regime axis the other two candidates condition on. Solo feasible (public histories, SJC's public harness). Lab: Compact-Bench's authors hold 106 production compaction chains and 14 backbones and could run this in a week; the re-open test is asking them. Dropped: a hindsight writer arm (the writer sees the receiver's remaining request) is a different question, closer to L2's learnable target (the 27.4-point full-history-to-target-state gap, Table 3), filed as a note for the claims stage, not a candidate.

scorecard.target_value: In print: 2610.31778, 'the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions' (omission by compaction count; the commission analogue is unmeasured); SJC's per-section unsourced census; Compact-Bench's 'successive production compactions' (106 chains). Who pays: every harness that compacts (Claude Code, Codex, OpenHands, OpenClaw), deciding whether to re-summarize from the raw log at the cost of prefill tokens; compaction evaluators deciding whether to report by boundary index.

impact_ceiling.floor: A two-regime unsourced-rate table with boundary curves on two corpora. Requires the two arms. Judgment p 0.5.
impact_ceiling.middle: The boundary-indexed invention curve adopted by one compaction benchmark (Compact-Bench's chains) and rewrite-from-raw tested in one harness. Requires a production corpus. Judgment p 0.3.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The write regime, not the gate, becomes the field's explanation of unsourced persistence and CL-W43-05 is rewritten around it. Requires replication on a second writer and the production chains. Judgment p 0.15.

title: Re-solve what the agent shipped: the per-command physics audit on agent-written simulators
statement: Re-run the paper's released code policies (the family that succeeds on 96.7% of 2,048 gift-box states, sec. 6.3, and its siblings on five other simulations) inside the shipped simulators with full physical state logged at every command boundary, then re-solve each command from its logged start state under a refined reference (the same solver with the time step halved and the solver-iteration cap and substep count doubled, relative to the agent-chosen settings in Table 6) and compute the lane's audit $d_k = \lVert F_{\mathrm{ref}}(x_k, a_k) - x_{k+1} \rVert$ on the verifier's state coordinates, with the threshold $\kappa$ set to the verifier's own success tolerance; separately run every episode end to end under the refined settings and report the success flip $\Delta S = S_{\mathrm{ship}} - S_{\mathrm{ref}}$ with its replay-seed interval. Six simulations, one per engine family in Table 6: rigid and articulated contact on Newton 1.5 with the MuJoCo Warp solver (0.5 ms ticks; the padlock at 1,920 Hz and 64 iterations), DFSPH liquid (93,750 to 348,160 particles), MPM soil, backward-Euler cloth, explicit FEM tissue (1e-5 s substeps, 73,273 tets), and the 7.18 M-cell welding enthalpy solver. Readouts per simulation: the distribution of $d_k / \kappa$ over contact-bearing commands, the share of return on suspicious commands $\rho = \sum_k r_k \mathbb{1}[d_k > \kappa] / \sum_k r_k$, and $\Delta S$.
claim: Agent-written simulators that pass same-model audits ship at discretisations their own solution policies depend on: halving the time step at the agent-chosen settings flips at least one in ten verified successes on at least two of six engine families.
trick: Take the robot programs that solve the agent-built tasks, re-run every move with the physics computed twice as finely, and count how many solved tasks stop being solved.
why_now: The card paper (2026-10-29) is the first released corpus of simulators whose physics a coding agent wrote: 25 simulators with their solver settings tabulated (Table 6), released solution programs with privileged state (sec. 6.3), and a recorded-attempt format with launch configuration and source version (Appendix D), so re-solving visited states under a refined reference is a replay job. The lane's audit (themes.yaml L5) has existed as a spec since 2026-10-11 with no agent-written corpus to run on. The refinement test itself is textbook (halve the step, compare), which is the flag: nothing is new but the target.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 (zero dollars, 2 days): clone the release; for each of the six simulations extract the step size $h$, iteration cap $K$ and substep count $m$ from Table 6 and the launch configuration; replay one recorded attempt twice from its command log and report the batch-repeat spread $\sigma_0$ of the final state as the resolution floor (checklist 2026-10-20: a GPU-batch repeat spread is read before any $d_k$); confirm that the verifier reads a state tolerance and record it as $\kappa$ per task. Step 1 (shipped arm): run the released code policy on 50 varied initial states per simulation with the full physical state saved at every command boundary; this is the arm the paper reports. Step 2 (reference arm, per command): from each saved start state, execute the same command under $(h/2, 2K, 2m)$ and compute $d_k$ on the verifier's coordinates; a command is 'contact-bearing' if the shipped solver reports any active contact or particle-boundary interaction during it. Step 3 (reference arm, end to end): run the same 50 initial states under $(h/2, 2K, 2m)$ from start to finish and score with the unchanged verifier; $\Delta S$ with a bootstrap interval over initial states and over replay seeds. Step 4: a second reference at $(h/4, 4K, 4m)$ on the two simulations with the largest $d_k$, to show $d_k$ shrinks with refinement (a convergence check, not a trend read from two points). Budget: the liquids and the welding cell at up to 200x real time dominate; 50 episodes x about 20 commands x 6 simulations at two refinement levels, about 120 GPU-hours on one H100-class card.
killing_experiment.kills_if: On all six simulations the median $d_k / \kappa$ over contact-bearing commands is below 0.1, $\rho < 0.05$, and $\Delta S$ lies inside the replay-seed interval of zero: the agent-chosen settings are converged on the states its own solutions visit, 'self-consistent' is also 'numerically converged' for this corpus, and the output is the first independent verification of agent-written solvers, a positive result the paper's authors and every group training on the 175 environments would cite.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.5: at least two of six simulations show $\Delta S \ge 10$ points and median $d_k > \kappa$ on contact-bearing commands, with the liquid (up to 348,160 particles) and the explicit FEM tissue (1e-5 s substeps, both run at or near the 200x-slower-than-real-time bound of Appendix B) the two that flip; the rigid Newton / MuJoCo Warp simulations at 0.5 ms ticks show $\Delta S$ near zero and $d_k$ below the batch-repeat floor on most commands.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: The card paper's physics evidence is a count: 'Physics checks count the named experiments in each simulation's report that test its physics against theory, measurement, or expected behavior' (Appendix E; 6 to 18 per simulation, Tables 1 and 6), with one named convergence check in 25 ('ink timestep and resolution convergence', whiteboard, Table 6); its speed auditor 'requires that a simulation run at most 200 times slower than real time' (Appendix B); its headline quality number is a 76% physics win rate from a same-model blind comparison (Figure 9, sec. 6.4). The paper treats a simulation that passes the ten criteria as realistic and never re-solves a visited state at a finer setting.
preregistered_surprise.would_change: If successes flip: the paper's 200 verifier-scored environments carry a discretisation dependence their audit cannot see, every result on them (the 0% headline, the 53% $\pi_{0.5}$ transfer) is conditional on the agent-chosen settings, and the GDP-coverage objective $F_Q(S)$ counts coverage of physics that changes under refinement; the lane's claim that speed bounds buy physics gains a second actor (a coding agent under a speed criterion) beside engine builders. If nothing flips: a coding agent choosing its own settings under a speed bound lands on converged numerics, which narrows CL-W43-01's actor to shipped engine defaults and removes the numerics half of the realism objection to agent-written physics, leaving only validation against reality (the third candidate from this card).

identifiability: Deterministic given: source version, launch configuration, seed and command sequence (Appendix D records all four), so the per-command re-solve has no luck term and its only noise is the GPU-batch repeat spread $\sigma_0$, which step 0 reports as the floor. The per-command audit starts every reference solve from the shipped state and does not compound; the end-to-end refined run does compound, so $\Delta S$ mixes convergence error with sensitive dependence on initial conditions in contact-rich scenes; the pair of readouts separates them (large $\Delta S$ with small $d_k$ reads as sensitivity, not non-convergence, and is reported as such). The code policy is a program (temperature zero by construction); no LLM is in the loop at run time. The reference is a proxy for convergence, not for reality (lane kill test 3); a simulation can pass this audit with a wrong contact model, and the third candidate from this card is the validation leg. The verifier is a state-based verifier, not a judge; $\kappa$ is its tolerance, read from code, not calibrated by us.
positioning_note: Solo: public code, 120 GPU-hours, no artifact needed. Lab: the Gym-Anything authors or an engine team run it on all 25 with the audit loop's own harness; the re-open test is whether the authors add a refinement criterion themselves. Dropped operators: operator 1 (replace the LLM blind judge with a cross-model judge and report chance-corrected agreement) is an LLM-judge self-preference footnote whose negative teaches nothing; operator 3 (allocate audit rounds per simulation by $d_k$ instead of a fixed three) presupposes this result.

scorecard.target_value: In print: the card paper's own warning that 'any such exploit could otherwise become learned behavior' (sec. 3) with no reference-based check of any simulation; themes.yaml L5 names the per-step audit on visited states as the lane's instrument and lists 'one-step checks do not compound' as its design rule; GPUSimBench (2607.13059, themes.yaml) measures GPU simulators at fixed settings and never sweeps them. Who pays: every group that trains RL on the 175 training environments (the paper's stated purpose, sec. 2); the Gym-Anything authors, whose next version can add a refinement criterion to the audit loop at zero cost; engine teams whose solvers (Newton 1.5, MuJoCo Warp) run under agent-chosen caps here.

impact_ceiling.floor: A six-row table of $d_k$ distributions and $\Delta S$ on agent-written simulators, with the convergence check; cited by the next agent-built-simulator paper as the verification they then add. Requires steps 0 to 4. Judgment p 0.5.
impact_ceiling.middle: Successes flip on the soft-body solvers: a refinement criterion enters the Gym-Anything audit loop, the 25-simulator release gains a per-simulation convergence column, and the lane's audit has its first corpus result on solvers nobody hand-tuned. Requires the probe plus a two-page note to the authors. Judgment p 0.35.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The audit becomes the verification standard for agent-written physics generally (the Gym-Anything software line, GenSim and RoboGen descendants that write solvers), reported beside the verifier score on every such release; requires running it on all 25 simulations and one more agent-written corpus, about 400 GPU-hours. Judgment p 0.15.

scorecard.relevance: Robotics and learning faculty (L5 route): direct, a verification result on the newest simulator corpus. Engine builders (Newton / Warp): direct, their solver under agent-chosen caps. Systems route: low, no scheduler. L1 (benchmark validity): moderate, the 0% headline's conditioning. LLM-agent lanes (L2, L3, L4): zero. Industry: anyone buying agent-built simulation. Jacob's edge: high, convergence under refinement, GPU batched solvers, conservation checks are his tools; no mechanical engineering is needed or implied.
scorecard.kill_probe: Six simulations, 50 initial states each, per-command re-solve at $(h/2, 2K, 2m)$ and end-to-end refined runs, a second refinement level on the two worst; about 120 GPU-hours, about $300, 10 days; dead if median $d_k / \kappa < 0.1$, $\rho < 0.05$ and $\Delta S$ inside the seed interval of zero on all six.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: From the card's fetched neighbors: GenSim (2310.01361) and RoboGen (2311.01455) generate tasks on fixed engines and verify by inspection or policy success, no refinement check; Gym-Anything for software (2604.06126) audits evidence against a checklist, no physics; RGBench (2511.06434, abstract fetched 2026-11-01) and GAUGE (2608.05948, abstract fetched 2026-11-01) validate against real data, not against refinement. From themes.yaml: GPUSimBench holds settings fixed; GPUPhysBench grades agent code against expert code, not against a refined solve of itself; Ostrich (2609.08800) sweeps the time step for one wheeled scene with no policy. Occupied by the card: the simulators, the verifiers, the code policies, the audit loop and the 76% win rate. Nobody in the fetched set re-solves an agent-written simulator's visited states under refinement; absence of a hit is not evidence, and the kill search must use the authors' words (physics checks, audit, adversarial auditor, timestep convergence, resolution convergence, defect, exploit) and the numerics words (Richardson, step-size convergence, verification). Race flag: the Gym-Anything team (CMU) can add this to their loop in a week.
scorecard.why_now: Card paper 2026-10-29 (25 released agent-written simulators with tabulated settings and released solution programs); the lane's audit spec 2026-10-11. The refinement test is textbook; the flag is recorded.
scorecard.register_and_not: Measurement (verification of numerics on a shipped corpus) with a recipe consequence (a refinement criterion in the audit loop). It is not a new simulator, not a fidelity benchmark, not a sim-to-real study (the reference is a finer solve, not reality), and not a judgment of the paper's LLM-controller results.

neighbors_to_check_first: 2610.40565 Table 6, Appendix B and Appendix D — the exact solver settings per simulation, the speed criterion, and whether the recorded attempt format includes enough state to replay deterministically
2607.13059 — GPUSimBench: whether any table varies the time step or solver iterations on the same scene; its repeat-run divergence is the floor this probe reports
2609.35639 — GPUPhysBench: whether its correctness oracle includes a refinement or convergence test on agent-written solvers, or only matching expert reference code
2609.08800 — Ostrich: the time-step sweep against real trajectories; whether any policy-visited-state audit exists there
2304.06372 — contact model comparison: residual-based accuracy criteria on fixed scenes; vocabulary for the kill search
headline_test: Coding agents that write their own physics ship it under-converged: on a counted share of agent-written simulators, the released solution programs' verified successes do not survive halving the time step.
claim_attachment_note: Tests the speed-for-physics clause of CL-W43-01 where the setting chooser is a coding agent under an explicit speed criterion (at most 200x real time) rather than an engine builder; the evaluate-in-refined row of the lane's 2x2 for policies written in the shipped simulator. The claims stage decides whether to widen CL-W43-01's actor or spin a claim on agent-written physics; the probe also supplies the scene set that CL-W43-J06's synthesised half would need verified before use.
