title: Optimise against the verifier: what a budgeted search finds that three adversarial audit rounds did not
statement: On four of the 25 simulations (two whose shared audit memory and reports record no remaining defect after round three, two whose recorded defect was fixed; Appendix B), run a budgeted derivative-free search (CMA-ES over the released code policy's waypoint, timing and force parameters, 600 episodes per task, privileged state as the paper's own learning studies allow) that maximises the state-based verifier's reward $r \in [0,1]$, and audit every verifier success with four physics invariants that need no reference engine: maximum interpenetration depth, conservation of particle mass and volume for liquids and soil, mechanical energy gained without actuator work, and the per-command refinement check $d_k$ of the sibling candidate. Report the physically invalid success share $\epsilon = \frac{\#\{\text{success} \wedge \text{violation}\}}{\#\{\text{success}\}}$ for the optimised programs against the same share for the released honest programs, with violation thresholds set at the 99th percentile of the honest programs' trajectories, and the recall of the paper's adversarial auditor: the share of violation classes the optimiser reaches that appear in that simulation's audit report or the shared memory.
claim: Adversarial LLM auditing before optimisation misses what a budgeted optimiser finds after it: in agent-written simulators that passed three audit rounds, a 600-episode search against the state-based verifier makes at least one in ten verified successes physically invalid.
trick: Instead of asking a model to imagine how a robot could cheat the simulator, let a cheap optimiser try to maximise the task score, then check whether its winning runs broke mass, energy or solid walls.
why_now: The card paper (2026-10-29) is the first corpus where an adversary's findings are written down per simulation before release (the adversarial auditor 'found a real defect in about three quarters of our simulations', sec. 6.4; the shared memory records 'colliders that passed audits and appeared in renders while having no physical effect', Appendix B), so an auditor's recall against an optimiser is computable for the first time; the released solution programs give the optimiser a parametrised starting point so no policy has to be learned. Policy-Aware Simulator Learning (2605.29032, abstract fetched 2026-11-01) states for learned simulators that 'powerful RL optimizers inevitably exploit minor model inaccuracies' and that the worst-case policy is dual to RL on one-step error; the engineered-simulator version with a written pre-release audit to score against is what this corpus supplies.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 (zero dollars, 2 days): read the 25 audit reports and the shared memory (Appendix B) and tabulate, per simulation, the defect classes found and fixed and the round-three verdict; choose two simulations recorded defect-free and two with a fixed defect, spanning rigid contact, liquid and cloth; read each verifier to confirm it scores state, not images. Step 1 (honest arm): run the released code policy on 200 varied initial states per simulation with full state logged; compute the four invariants per trajectory and set each violation threshold at the honest arm's 99th percentile (so $\epsilon_{\mathrm{honest}} \le 0.01$ by construction on the calibration set; report it on a held-out 100 states). Step 2 (optimiser arm): parametrise the code policy's waypoints, timings and commanded forces (10 to 40 parameters), run CMA-ES for 600 episodes per simulation with the verifier reward as the objective and the same varied initial states, log full state, compute the invariants on every verifier success; $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}$ with a bootstrap interval over episodes. Step 3 (recall): two labellers with a written rubric sort each optimiser violation into a class (interpenetration, through-collider, mass loss, energy gain, discretisation-dependent) and mark whether that class appears in the simulation's audit report or the memory; report agreement and the auditor's recall per simulation. Cost: 4 simulations x 900 episodes at about 2 minutes each (the paper's code-policy run time, sec. 6.3) plus the refinement re-solves on successes, about 100 GPU-hours.
killing_experiment.kills_if: On all four simulations $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} - \epsilon_{\mathrm{honest}} < 0.05$ with the bootstrap band including zero: a 600-episode optimiser against the verifier reaches no exploit the three-round audit left, the paper's trust story holds at this budget, and the result is a positive verification of LLM adversarial auditing that the authors and anyone building creation-audit loops would cite.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.55: $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} \ge 0.1$ on at least two of four simulations including one recorded defect-free, with interpenetration and through-collider violations (the memory file's own class) the majority, and the auditor's recall below 0.5 on those two; near zero on the rigid-contact simulation where the Newton / MuJoCo Warp solver was not written by the agent.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: The card paper: 'Since reinforcement learning optimizes against the simulation, any such exploit could otherwise become learned behavior' (sec. 3), answered by an adversarial auditor with legal robot actions over three rounds whose residual miss rate is never estimated; the simulations that survive are shipped as RL environments and no RL is run on them (sec. 6, Appendix B). Policy-Aware Simulator Learning (2605.29032) assumes exploitation is inevitable for learned models and does not measure engineered ones.
preregistered_surprise.would_change: If $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}$ is large: pre-release LLM auditing is a low-recall exploit search, the 200 environments need an optimiser-in-the-loop audit before RL, and the ruler the lane wants for soft bodies (where no converged reference exists) is the invariant-violation share under a budgeted optimiser, which this probe operationalises. If $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} \approx 0$: three rounds of model-imagined legal actions are as good as 600 episodes of optimisation at finding exploits, which argues for the loop as a cheap verification standard and against spending GPU-hours on adversarial search for agent-audited simulators.

identifiability: Exploitable given: the budget (600 episodes), the search space (the released program's parameters) and the verifier; $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}}$ is a property of (simulation, verifier, parametrisation, budget) and is reported as such, never as 'the' exploitability. Violations are defined by invariants readable from the privileged state the paper exposes (penetration depth, particle counts and volumes, kinetic plus potential energy against actuator work), with thresholds from the honest arm's 99th percentile, so $\epsilon_{\mathrm{honest}}$ is near 0.01 by construction and the quantity of interest is the difference. Deterministic replay given source version, configuration and seed (Appendix D), so the optimiser's noise is the varied initial states, which both arms share. The auditor's recall depends on a class taxonomy: two labellers, a written rubric, agreement reported; a class is 'found' only if it appears in that simulation's own report or the memory text. Verifier, not judge: the objective is the state-based verifier; no LLM scores anything in this probe.
positioning_note: Solo: public code, 100 GPU-hours, an off-the-shelf optimiser. Lab: the Gym-Anything authors run the optimiser auditor as a fourth role inside the loop on all 25, which is the re-open test (ask whether they have run any optimiser against their verifiers). Operator 2 moves the exploit search from before optimisation (a model's imagination) to after it; operator 7 turns the paper's adversarial auditor into a control arm scored by recall. Not written: operator 3 (allocate audit rounds by measured exploitability) presupposes this result; a learned RL policy as the adversary was rejected because the brief forbids a new learned model and the code-policy parametrisation is cheaper.

scorecard.target_value: In print: the card paper's sec. 3 warning and its sec. 6.4 defect rate; 2605.29032's statement that optimisers 'inevitably exploit minor model inaccuracies'; themes.yaml L5 names 'simulator overoptimization' and 'what policies exploit' as the lane's question and SAPU (2305.17110) as the precedent where interpenetration was exploited and had to be filtered. Who pays: groups about to train RL on the 175 environments; the Gym-Anything authors (an optimiser-in-the-loop fourth auditor); benchmark users who read the verifier's success bit as physical competence.

impact_ceiling.floor: A four-row table of invalid-success shares under optimisation with the auditor's recall, on the first agent-written corpus; cited by the next creation-audit paper when it adds an optimiser auditor. Requires steps 0 to 3. Judgment p 0.5.
impact_ceiling.middle: Recall below 0.5 on audited-clean simulations: the creation-audit loop gains a budgeted-optimiser auditor, the invariant-violation share becomes the reported exploitability number for soft-body simulators, and CL-W43-J03's optimiser-side instrument has its first corpus result. Requires the probe plus the auditor's code released. Judgment p 0.3.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The optimiser audit becomes a standard column on agent-built and hand-built soft-body benchmarks (RGBench, GAUGE, BEHAVIOR-1K descendants), with the auditor's recall as the number that grades LLM audits; requires the audit on all 25 simulations plus one incumbent suite, about 500 GPU-hours. Judgment p 0.15.

scorecard.relevance: Robotics and learning faculty: direct. Engine builders: moderate, the exploits are in agent-written solvers more than in their kernels. L1 (benchmark validity): direct, a verifier's success bit versus physical validity. L2: zero (no training dynamics). Systems route: zero. Industry: anyone deploying creation-audit loops. Jacob's edge: high on the invariants (mass, energy, penetration are conservation checks), moderate on the optimiser (off-the-shelf CMA-ES), zero on LLM-audit design.
scorecard.kill_probe: Four simulations, honest arm 200 states plus 100 held out, CMA-ES 600 episodes each, invariant audit on successes, rubric labelling; about 100 GPU-hours, about $250, 10 days; dead if $\epsilon_{\mathrm{opt}} - \epsilon_{\mathrm{honest}} < 0.05$ with the band including zero on all four.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: From fetched abstracts: 2605.29032 (Policy-Aware Simulator Learning) proves the worst-case policy is dual to RL on the critic's one-step error and measures it on learned models in continuous control, not on engineered simulators and not against a written audit; from themes.yaml: SAPU (2305.17110) documents interpenetration exploitation in Isaac and filters it, no optimiser audit; from the card: the adversarial auditor is the paper's own pre-optimisation exploit search with its recall unestimated. Occupied by the card: the auditor design, the defect rate, the memory file. CL-W43-J03 (thought) names the budgeted-optimiser violation as its predictor; CL-W44-J02 (thought) rests on the premise that checks miss exploits; neither has a corpus result and this probe serves both without being either. Race flag: the Gym-Anything team and the 2605.29032 group; density to be counted at the kill search in the authors' words (adversarial auditor, legal actions, defect, exploit, simulation hacking, reward hacking in simulation, worst-case policy, penetration).
scorecard.why_now: Card paper 2026-10-29 (written per-simulation audit findings; released solution programs as optimiser seeds); 2605.29032 (2026-05) for the duality framing. The optimiser is old; the flag is recorded.
scorecard.register_and_not: Measurement (exploitability under a budget, and an auditor's recall) with a recipe consequence (an optimiser auditor in the loop). It is not RL training, not a new auditor design, not a learned model, and not a sim-to-real result; a violation is a broken invariant inside the simulator, not a gap to reality.

neighbors_to_check_first: 2610.40565 Appendix B and sec. 6.4 — the adversarial auditor's protocol, the memory file's defect classes, and which simulations are recorded defect-free after round three
2605.29032 — Policy-Aware Simulator Learning: whether any experiment runs the adversarial policy against an engineered (non-learned) simulator; its definition of exploitation
2305.17110 — IndustReal / SAPU: the interpenetration thresholds and the share of episodes exploited, as the precedent and the vocabulary
2604.06126 — Gym-Anything for software: whether its audit loop estimates its own miss rate or runs any optimiser against its verifiers
2608.06088 — IcFuzz (listed in CL-W43-J03's thread): fuzzing Isaac Sim for crashes; whether it scores physical validity or only crashes
headline_test: Pre-release LLM adversarial auditing of agent-written simulators has low recall against a budgeted optimiser: a counted share of verified successes become physically invalid once a cheap search optimises against the verifier.
claim_attachment_note: Orphan by honesty: the sentence it tests is about LLM audit recall, which no open claim states. It supplies the optimiser-side instrument of CL-W43-J03 (worst-case violation a budgeted optimiser extracts) on a corpus with no robot, and tests the 'checks cannot see' premise of CL-W44-J02 on a case where the check is an LLM auditor; the claims stage decides whether to lift it as its own claim or attach it to J03 if J03's headline is widened from transfer prediction to audit recall.

title: Score the agent's cloth and tissue against measured reality: GAUGE's trajectory error on agent-written solvers
statement: Port three of GAUGE's measurement-grounded task families (2608.05948: one textile, one volumetric deformable, one rigid impulsive contact, each with real trajectories, calibrated material metadata and a task observable) into the shipped agent-written solvers (the backward-Euler cloth, the explicit FEM tissue, and the Newton 1.5 / MuJoCo Warp rigid stack the agent configured), feed GAUGE's calibrated parameters as inputs, and compute GAUGE's generalized trajectory error $e = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T} \lVert q^{\mathrm{sim}}_t - q^{\mathrm{real}}_t \rVert$ over the task observable $q_t$ at the $T$ measured instants, placing each number on GAUGE's own table beside Isaac Sim, Genesis and Newton; before scoring, validate the port by reproducing GAUGE's published Newton number within 10% through the same scene files. Readouts: the agent solver's error relative to the best and worst of the three engines per family, and the error of the agent solver run at GAUGE's calibrated parameters versus at the parameters the agent chose for itself.
claim: Agent-written soft-body solvers that win 76% of same-model blind comparisons are further from measured real deformable trajectories than the shipped engines they beat, on the same real data and the same error metric.
trick: Run the agent's cloth and tissue physics on scenes where somebody filmed and measured the real material, and read its error off the same ruler three shipped engines were already scored with.
why_now: GAUGE (2608.05948, published 2026-08-06; abstract fetched 2026-11-01) supplies 'real-world trajectories ... paired with calibrated physical metadata' across 'rigid bodies, flexible cables, textiles, and volumetric deformable objects' and already scores Isaac Sim, Genesis and Newton on 14 families with 'generalized trajectory errors', so the incumbents' side of the comparison is published; the card paper (2026-10-29) supplies released soft-body solvers written by an agent and compared to incumbents only by a same-model blind judgment (sec. 6.4). The card notes the creator cites GAUGE's material tables for static parameters and never uses a measured trajectory, so the comparison is open and the inputs are already in the agent's hands.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 (zero dollars, 3 days): confirm GAUGE's release of trajectories, metadata and scene definitions for at least one textile, one volumetric-deformable and one rigid-contact family, and its exact error definition; confirm in the agent-written reports which solver each simulation uses and whether any GAUGE trajectory was used in creation or audit (the card says only static parameters were cited; this is checked, not assumed). Step 1 (port validation): build the three scenes for Newton through our own scene files and reproduce GAUGE's published Newton error within 10%; if the port misses by more, fix the port before touching the agent solver, so scene error is bounded before solver error is read. Step 2: run the agent's cloth, tissue and rigid stacks on the same scenes at GAUGE's calibrated parameters, compute $e$ per family with GAUGE's uncertainty annotations as the error bar; Step 3: repeat at the agent's self-chosen parameters from its own report to separate parameter choice from solver form. Step 4: the refinement check of the sibling candidate on the same runs, so model-form error (persists under refinement) is separated from discretisation error (shrinks under refinement). Cost: porting labour dominates; GPU use is small (tens of short scenes).
killing_experiment.kills_if: On every ported family the agent solver's error $e$ at GAUGE's calibrated parameters lies inside the range spanned by Isaac Sim, Genesis and Newton on that family (with the port validated to 10% on Newton): the headline is dead, and the result is the first evidence that an agent-written solver audited without real data reaches validated-engine parity on measured deformable trajectories, a bigger result for the paper than its own 76%, and a direct update to the lane's belief that synthesised soft-body scenes carry no measured material behaviour.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.6: on the textile family the agent's cloth error is 1.5x to 3x the best engine's (GAUGE reports 'the largest discrepancies arising in impulsive contact, rapid textile motion, and volumetric deformation' even for shipped engines, and the agent's cloth was checked only against formulas and expected behaviour); on the rigid impulsive-contact family the agent stack lands within the engine range because the solver underneath is Newton 1.5 / MuJoCo Warp, not agent-written; the volumetric family sits between.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: The card paper: its quality evidence is a 76% physics win rate and an 80% visuals win rate from a blind comparison where 'Claude Opus 5.5 then compared each pair blind' against incumbents including RGBench and BEHAVIOR-1K (sec. 6.4, Table 2), and its physics checks test 'against theory, measurement, or expected behavior' with no simulation compared to a measured trajectory (Appendix E). The lane's standing belief (CL-W43-J06 thread, 2026-10-23 session) is the opposite: 'synthesised soft-body scenes carry no measured material behaviour'. One of the two is wrong on this corpus.
preregistered_surprise.would_change: If the agent solvers are far worse: the 76% is a same-model preference over reports and videos, the blind-judge protocol is retired as a fidelity claim, and agent-built soft-body suites are scene generators that need a validation column from GAUGE-class data before policies trained in them are reported; the lane's 'ground truth from reality' direction is confirmed with a number. If they reach parity: the audit loop produces validated-grade soft-body physics from formulas and self-run checks alone, the J06 synthesised half is usable as the suite's scene set, and the validation leg of the lane's V&V triad can be run on agent-written solvers at the same cost as on engines.

identifiability: The error $e$ is a property of (solver, scene port, parameters, GAUGE trajectory); step 1 bounds the port's contribution by reproducing a published engine number within 10% through the same scene files, and step 3 separates the agent's parameter choices from its solver form, so a reading above the engine range is attributed to the solver only after both controls pass. Contamination: GAUGE predates the card paper and the creator cites its material tables (card information_asymmetry), so step 0 reads the 25 reports for any use of GAUGE trajectories; static parameters in hand and trajectories unseen is the expected and reported condition. GAUGE's uncertainty annotations are the error bar; no LLM judges anything. The comparison is at calibrated parameters, not tuned ones, for every engine alike, matching GAUGE's protocol. Deterministic scenes; the refinement check in step 4 tells model-form error (does not shrink) from discretisation error (shrinks), which the sibling candidate measures on the task scenes.
positioning_note: Solo: public data (if GAUGE's release is confirmed in step 0; otherwise RGBench's measured garment dynamics are the fallback for the textile family), released solvers, 10 GPU-hours. Lab: the GAUGE team adds the rows with their own harness in days, which is the re-open test (ask whether they will score agent-written solvers). Operator 5 is the matched comparison the paper did not run (same real trajectories, same metric, the three engines already scored); operator 6 is the validation leg of verification-and-validation from computational engineering, mapped as: verification asks whether the equations are solved right (the sibling candidate), validation asks whether the right equations are solved (this one). Not written: running the creation-audit loop on a GAUGE scene, which is the card's own method on a new benchmark and is forbidden by the brief.

scorecard.target_value: In print: GAUGE's abstract states existing fidelity evaluations 'rely heavily on perceptual similarity or human judgments' and finds 'no uniformly faithful physics engine'; the card paper's realism evidence is exactly a model's judgment over reports and videos; RGBench (2511.06434, abstract fetched 2026-11-01) built 'a comprehensive protocol to evaluate garment simulation quality with carefully measured real garment dynamics' and is the only incumbent in the card's Table 2 with such a check; themes.yaml L5 lists validation against real impact data as the second instrument and 'higher fidelity is not reality' as a kill test. Who pays: groups choosing between an agent-built suite and RGBench / GAUGE-validated engines for deformable policies; the Gym-Anything authors (a validation column); the GAUGE team (a new row class: agent-written solvers).

impact_ceiling.floor: Three rows added to GAUGE's table for agent-written solvers, with the port validated on Newton; cited whenever agent-built soft-body physics is quoted as realistic. Requires steps 0 to 3. Judgment p 0.55.
impact_ceiling.middle: A validation column becomes part of the creation-audit loop's release criteria (a GAUGE family per material class), and the lane's validation instrument has its first corpus result on solvers nobody hand-tuned. Requires the probe plus the refinement separation of step 4. Judgment p 0.3.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The standard for any agent-written simulator release: verification (the sibling candidate) plus validation (this one) reported per simulation; a reviewer's ask in robot learning. Requires all GAUGE families on all applicable agent solvers, about 60 GPU-hours and two months of porting. Judgment p 0.15.

scorecard.relevance: Robotics and learning faculty: direct. Engine builders (Newton, Genesis, Isaac): direct, their rows are the comparison. L1 (benchmark validity): direct, the blind-judge win rate as a validity question. Systems route, L2, L3, L4: zero. Industry: buyers of agent-built simulation. Jacob's edge: moderate to high (numerics, conservation checks and the refinement separation in step 4 are his; the scene porting is engineering labour).
scorecard.kill_probe: Three GAUGE families ported to the agent's cloth, tissue and rigid stacks after a 10% port validation on Newton; about 10 GPU-hours, about $50, 12 days of mostly porting; dead if the agent solver's error lies within the Isaac / Genesis / Newton range on every family.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: From fetched abstracts: GAUGE (2608.05948) scores Isaac Sim, Genesis and Newton on 14 families and six video models, not agent-written solvers; RGBench (2511.06434) scores its own cloth simulator against measured garment dynamics; from the card: the paper compares to RGBench and others only by same-model blind judgment and cites GAUGE's material tables without using a trajectory. From themes.yaml: Acosta et al. (RA-L 2022) found elastic impacts wrong in Drake, MuJoCo and Bullet, the rigid precedent. Occupied: the GAUGE protocol and numbers (we add rows, we do not build a benchmark); the card's solvers. Nobody in the fetched set has scored an agent-written solver against a measured trajectory; the kill search must use GAUGE's and RGBench's words (measurement-grounded, physical fidelity, trajectory error, calibrated metadata, real garment dynamics) and the card's (physics checks, realistic, blind comparison). Race flag: the GAUGE team (an obvious new row class) and the Gym-Anything team.
scorecard.why_now: GAUGE 2026-08-06 (real trajectories, calibrated metadata, engine baselines on the same metric); card paper 2026-10-29 (released agent-written soft-body solvers). Both enabling pieces are under three months old.
scorecard.register_and_not: Measurement (validation against real data on a published metric) with a standards consequence (a validation column on agent-written releases). It is not a new benchmark, not a new simulator, not a sim-to-real policy study, and not a judgment of the paper's RL or LLM-controller results; the port is the whole labour and its validation on Newton is what makes the number about the solver and not about us.

title: Old because it is old, or old because it is true? Counterbalanced and unfamiliar-entity arms of the obsolete-fact swap
statement: Rebuild the card paper's 74 paired conflict questions from the public MemoryAgentBench FactConsolidation 6K split and rerun its equal-size swap (condition $A = \{s^{+}, u_1, u_2, u_3\}$ against $B = \{s^{-}, s^{+}, u_1, u_2\}$, where $s^{+}$ is the latest statement about the target relation, $s^{-}$ its older version and $u_j$ unrelated statements) under three value assignments at matched prompt size: original (the obsolete value is the ordinary-world fact and the latest is synthetic, as in all 50 flips of the paper's Table 17), counterbalanced (the two values swap roles, so the world fact is the latest and the synthetic value the obsolete), and unfamiliar (the subject entity is replaced by a fictional name in every statement and in the question, so neither value has a parametric anchor), with a question-only arm per assignment that reads the prior directly. Readers are the paper's Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Qwen3-14B plus Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, temperature 0, three draws of the unrelated statements per question; the outcome is the stale-selection rate $r_c$, the fraction of the 74 questions whose answer under condition $B$ matches the obsolete value, per assignment $c$. The decomposition $r_{\mathrm{orig}} = \rho + \pi_{-}$, $r_{\mathrm{unf}} = \rho$, $r_{\mathrm{cb}} = \rho - \pi_{+}$ reads $\rho$, the version-blindness rate (the reader picks the older of two in-context values when neither is backed by its weights), and $\pi_{\mp}$, the prior pull toward the world value when it is the older ($-$) or the newer ($+$) statement, off three cells the paper reports only one of.
claim: The obsolete-fact failure in agent-memory benchmarks is the reader's parametric prior winning over the context, not recency failing: when neither in-context value is a world fact the stale-selection rate falls below 15% on the same reader that shows 55%, so benchmarks that build 'updates' by replacing true facts with synthetic ones measure knowledge conflict, not memory.
trick: Swap which of the two competing values is the real-world fact, and separately make both values fictional, and see whether the reader still picks the older one.
why_now: The card paper (2610.36308, 2026-10-26) names both arms and runs neither ('establish susceptibility to these competitors, not that temporal obsolescence alone drives the effect', sec. 4), on a public split (MemoryAgentBench 2507.05257, Conflict_Resolution / FactConsolidation, released on Hugging Face) with a prompt and audit protocol specified in its App. A, so the three cells cost one afternoon of a single GPU; 2606.01435 (the paper's cited neighbour) already treats the same split as a 'freshness' task and reports 82 to 93% from pipeline separation, and 2610.41056 (2026-10-29) formalizes 'outdated memory' as a write-rule problem scored by evidence-conditioned accuracy, so the lane is building recipes on a benchmark whose stale value is always the true one.

killing_experiment.design: Step 1 (1 day, $0): download the 6K FactConsolidation history and questions, reconstruct the 74 single-older-version chains by the paper's App. A.5 chain labels, and for each question build the three assignments: original (statements as shipped), counterbalanced (exchange the object values of $s^{-}$ and $s^{+}$ while keeping their statement numbers, so the world fact now carries the higher number and is the gold), unfamiliar (replace the subject entity by a fictional name drawn from a fixed list in both statements and the question; both values kept, gold unchanged). Step 2 (1 day, about 4 GPU-hours on one 80 GB GPU via vLLM): for each assignment, each of 3 readers, conditions $A$ and $B$ and 3 draws of $u_j$ with zero content-word overlap, plus a question-only arm; about 4,400 calls of 160 to 300 prompt tokens with 64 output tokens. Score by the paper's normalized substring match against the chain values (latest / stale / unknown / other); report $r_c$ with a task-level bootstrap band over the 74 questions and the exact McNemar $p$ between original and each other assignment; report condition $A$ accuracy per assignment as the floor check (the paper's is 74/74). Optional step 3 (same cost again): render $s^{-}$ with an explicit '[superseded by #n]' tag in each assignment, the paper's own untested 'mark inactive' recommendation; its reading is a secondary readout for C-W43-09's premise (does a reader consume an explicit supersession mark) and enters no kill condition here.
killing_experiment.kills_if: On Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, $r_{\mathrm{unf}} \geq 0.40$ or $r_{\mathrm{cb}} \geq 0.40$ (within 15 points of the paper's $41/74 = 0.554$) with the bootstrap band above 0.30: the reader picks the older value without parametric help, version blindness is a reader property, the paper's temporal reading stands and the prior is a minor term. That outcome is citable as the first direct separation of recency from prior on an agent-memory benchmark and strengthens the lane's 'readers ignore version marks' sentence. Protocol kill: condition $A$ accuracy under the counterbalanced or unfamiliar assignment falls below 0.90 on the 7B reader, meaning the rewrite itself broke readability and the cells are not comparable; then the assignment is repaired before any reading.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.6: on the 7B reader $r_{\mathrm{unf}}$ is 0.05 to 0.15 and $r_{\mathrm{cb}}$ is 0.00 to 0.05 against $r_{\mathrm{orig}}$ near 0.55, so $\pi_{-}$ is at least two thirds of the paper's 55.4-point drop; on the 14B reader $r_{\mathrm{orig}} = 0.12$ collapses to under 0.03 in both other arms; the question-only arm answers the world value in over 60% of the 74 (the paper's question-only arm scores 0/74 against synthetic gold, Table 11, which is the same fact read the other way).
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: The card paper's abstract and sec. 3.2 read the swap as evidence that 'obsolete' entries override current ones, and sec. 4 recommends that memory systems 'retire, down-weight, or explicitly mark superseded facts as inactive'; MemoryAgentBench (2507.05257) files the split under 'selective forgetting' and 2606.01435 under 'freshness'; the paper itself concedes the confound in one sentence ('In this benchmark, obsolete values often match familiar world knowledge while the synthetic updates contradict it', sec. 4) and does not stratify. The knowledge-conflict literature predicts the opposite reading: 2305.13300 reports 'a strong confirmation bias when the external evidence contains some information that is consistent with their parametric memory, despite being presented with conflicting evidence at the same time', which is the swap's condition $B$ exactly.
preregistered_surprise.would_change: If the prior is most of the drop: every memory-update benchmark built by substituting synthetic values for true ones (FactConsolidation, and any update split that edits real-world facts) owes a counterbalanced or fictional-entity stratum before a 'stale memory' number is reported, memory-system write rules motivated by these numbers (delete or tag superseded facts) are motivated by a knowledge-conflict result, and for CL-W43-05 the only reader-side override evidence in the lane does not transfer to an agent's own stale notes, which have no parametric backing, so the claim's reader cell is untested rather than occupied. If version blindness survives without the prior: the reader cannot use a statement number as a recency mark, which is the strongest reader-side support the lane has for marking or deleting superseded entries at write time, and C-W43-09's tag arm inherits a cheap prior result (step 3).
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: Either $r_{\mathrm{unf}} \leq 0.15$ on the 7B reader (prior, not recency, is the mechanism; benchmark-validity consequence) or $r_{\mathrm{unf}} \geq 0.40$ (version blindness without a prior; write-time marking consequence); the uninformative band is 0.15 to 0.40, in which the two terms are comparable and the report says so with the decomposition.

scorecard.target_value: In print: the card paper names the arm and declines it (sec. 4, quoted above); 2305.13300's confirmation-bias finding is the competing explanation stated by its own authors; MemoryAgentBench's authors (2507.05257) label the split a memory competency. Who pays: benchmark owners of update and forgetting splits (MemoryAgentBench, LongMemEval's knowledge-update category 2410.10813, MemOps 2607.12893 whose abstract names 'relying on stale values after a correction' as a failure cause), memory-system builders whose write rules cite these numbers (Stashbird 2609.34242 'corrections supersede prior active relations'; 2610.41056's outdated-memory manager), and the CL-W43-05 thread, which needs to know whether the lane's reader-side override result is about recency at all.

impact_ceiling.floor: The three cells on one benchmark and three small readers; a note that corrects the card paper's reading one way or the other; requires steps 1 and 2; probability 0.4 (judgment).
impact_ceiling.middle: The decomposition identity plus the result that the prior is most of the drop, adopted as a required stratum (counterbalanced or fictional-entity) by one memory benchmark's update split; requires step 2 and one frontier reader via API (about $20); probability 0.4 (judgment).
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The same split applied to two more update benchmarks (LongMemEval knowledge updates, MemOps update probes) shows the published stale-memory rates are mostly prior pull, changing how memory-update numbers are reported across the lane; requires two more datasets and about 20 GPU-hours; probability 0.2 (judgment).

relevance.routes: L4 routes: memory-system groups (whether supersession must be enforced at write time or whether the reader is fine once the prior is removed); product teams (what a 'stale memory' number means on their benchmarks); Narasimhan's self-evolving interest, moderately (what a self-written memory's old entries do to the reader when the model has no prior on them). L1 secondary: benchmark validity of update splits.
relevance.industry: Direct for teams shipping memory layers that report update accuracy; the stratum is free to compute.
relevance.jacobs_edge: The decomposition identity is napkin algebra he can check; zero otherwise.

scorecard.kill_probe: Three assignments x two conditions x three draws x three readers on the public 74-question split; about 4 GPU-hours, about $10, 3 days; dead if the 7B reader's stale-selection rate stays at or above 0.40 with neither value a world fact (or with the world fact newest); protocol kill if condition $A$ accuracy under a rewritten assignment drops below 0.90.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: Occupied: the card paper's original-assignment cell and its budget sweep; 2606.01435's pipeline separation on the same split; pre-window precedents 2109.05052 (entity-substitution knowledge conflicts: models 'over-rely on memorized information' and a framework released to generate conflicts) and 2305.13300 (counter-memory construction; receptivity to coherent evidence; confirmation bias when any evidence matches the prior), 2302.00093 (irrelevant-context control). In window (arXiv API, obsolete/outdated/superseded/stale x memory/agent x parametric/prior/knowledge-conflict x recency/temporal/update: 56 total, 40 read by title, none on target for a counterbalanced arm on an agent-memory benchmark): STALE 2605.06527 (implicit invalidation, frontier models at 55.2%, no prior stratum in the abstract), MemOps 2607.12893 (lifecycle operations with gold traces; stale-after-correction as a named failure), 2610.41056 (outdated memory vs poisoning; evidence-conditioned accuracy; no prior stratum in the abstract), 2609.34242 Stashbird (supersession at write time). The card paper's authors are the natural owners and have the harness; the re-open test is asking whether their counterbalanced arm exists unpublished. Kill search owed in the neighbours' words: knowledge conflict, counter-memory, parametric, confirmation bias, counterfactual context, entity substitution, freshness, selective forgetting.
scorecard.why_now: Card paper 2026-10-26 names the arm; the split is public; 2610.41056 (2026-10-29) and 2606.01435 are building write rules and pipelines on numbers from this split in the same quarter.
scorecard.register_and_not: Missing comparison (the counterbalanced arm) in the measurement register, with a benchmark-validity consequence and a decomposition identity. Not a memory system, not a reader fine-tune, not the card's method on a new benchmark (same benchmark, the arm it declined).

identifiability: The stale-selection rate $r_c$ is random given (assignment, reader, draw of $u_j$) only through the reader's temperature-0 decode, which is deterministic per prompt on one serving stack, so the draws of $u_j$ and the three readers are the only variance sources and are reported as such; the 74 questions are the paper's fixed cohort, not a sample from a population, and the bootstrap band is over questions. The prior $\pi$ is a property of the (reader, entity) pair, not of the protocol, once the fictional-name list and the value-exchange rule are fixed and pre-registered; the question-only arm reads it directly. Normalized substring match carries the paper's documented false positives (App. I.1), which are symmetric across assignments and reported by count.
positioning_note: Solo is sufficient: public data, one GPU afternoon, no artifact; lab adds nothing but the authors' own harness. Lab-adjacent in the sense the lane requires: it grades a published reading and a benchmark split, not a recipe. Attached to CL-W43-05 because the card marks this paper as the claim's reader-side cell with the source present; the claims stage can re-attach it to an L1 benchmark-validity claim if 'readers ignore version marks' is judged outside CL-W43-05's sentence.
neighbors_to_check_first: 2610.36308 App. A.5 and Table 17 - confirm every one of the 50 flips has the world fact as the obsolete value (the card's reading) and that the chain labels suffice to rebuild the 74 pairs without the authors' code
2606.01435 - same split; read whether its 'freshness executor' ablation or any table stratifies by whether the stale value is the true one
2305.13300 - counter-memory construction and the confirmation-bias cell; whether any experiment places both a prior-consistent and a prior-inconsistent value in one context with an ordering rule
2109.05052 - entity substitution as the conflict generator; whether time-dependent queries were tested with both values present
2605.06527 (STALE) and 2607.12893 (MemOps) - whether either benchmark's update scenarios use real-world facts as the outdated state and whether a prior stratum is reported
2507.05257 (MemoryAgentBench) - how FactConsolidation's synthetic updates were generated and whether the authors note the world-fact confound
headline_test: Stale-memory failures reported on agent-memory benchmarks are the model's prior winning over the context, not recency failing: with no world fact in play the override rate collapses, so the lane's reader-side evidence for 'a stale entry beside the current one overrides it' does not transfer to an agent's own stale notes.
claim_attachment_note: tests whether the only reader-side override result the lane has (2610.36308) is a parametric-prior effect; if so the claim's reader cell is untested rather than occupied and 'readers ignore version marks' returns to open; if not, the lane gains a prior-free version-blindness result that supports write-time marking (C-W43-09's premise); the claims stage can detach to an L1 benchmark-validity claim

title: One wrong bullet in the agent's own summary, the right value in a fresh tool output: which one does the agent act on?
statement: Move the card paper's matched-size swap from a retrieved statement list read by a 7B model to a compaction summary read by a frontier agent in a closed loop: on AppWorld test-normal in the public SJC harness (ACON patch plus OpenClaw safeguard compressor, 4,096-token window, frozen agent; github.com/GuanghuiMin/sjc per C-W43-23's kill record), pre-select 60 tasks whose first state-changing reference call takes a literal argument (an id, email, amount or date) and whose first compaction boundary precedes that call, intercept the summary at that boundary, and insert one bullet of fixed length into its key-facts section under four matched-length contents: (U) an unrelated true fact, (S) a wrong value for that argument that an earlier environment output did contain (a sibling item from the same listing), (F) a wrong value no output ever contained, and (P) the same fabricated value written as the agent's own earlier decision ('Decided: use ... for this step'). In the main arms the harness then issues the read call that returns the current value as the first post-boundary turn, so the summary's wrong value and the environment's right value sit in the same context (the paper's condition $B$ with the summary as $s^{-}$); S and F are also run without the forced read. Score without a judge: uptake $u_c = \Pr[\text{the first post-boundary state-changing call uses the inserted value}]$ by exact normalized match, the natural re-read rate in the unforced arms, and task success, with three runs per cell.
claim: After compaction a frontier agent's own summary outranks a fresh tool output in the same context: when the two disagree on an argument the agent acts on the summary's value in more than half of runs, and no less often when no observation ever produced that value.
trick: Plant one wrong value in the agent's own compaction summary, let the environment show the right value right after, and count how often the agent acts on the summary anyway, with the planted value either something it once saw or something nothing ever produced.
why_now: The card paper (2026-10-26) shows the paired equal-size swap is a judge-free ruler for 'retrieved but overridden' and its card names the transfer to a compaction summary as the piece CL-W43-05 lacks; SJC (2610.20927, 2026-10-14) ships the harness and the compressor and reports that failed runs carry out summary entries, with no arm in which the environment contradicts the summary in view; 2606.25449 (2026-06-24) scores the same contest judge-free with an explicit correction and leaves the silent contradiction by a tool output untested; 2608.06057 (2026-08-06) shows polluted history flips 32.1% of decisions on a 1.7B model and stops at the history, not the self-written summary.

killing_experiment.design: Step 1 (about $100, 3 days): one Prompting run over 168 test-normal tasks (shared with C-W43-08 if it runs) to find tasks whose first boundary precedes the first literal-argument state-changing reference call; keep 60, pre-register the argument and its current value per task from the reference solution, the sibling value for S from the pre-boundary outputs, the fabricated value for F (same format, never printed), and one bullet wording per arm at matched token length. Step 2 (about $400, 6 days): six cells per task, U / S / F / P with the forced read and S / F without, three runs each: 1,080 continuations of 10 to 15 steps on the paper's GPT agent at its default temperature; the forced read is the reference solution's own read call, executed by the harness and appended as a normal tool turn. Compute $u_c$ per cell with a task-level bootstrap band (1,000 resamples), the paired difference $u_F - u_S$, the natural re-read rate and uptake conditional on it in the unforced arms, and success per cell; audit 50 exact-match labels by hand. Secondary: repeat S and F with forced read on MiniMax-M3 if the GPT result sits within 10 points of a kill boundary.
killing_experiment.kills_if: In the forced-read arms, $u_S$ and $u_F$ are both below 0.25 with bands under 0.35 (the fresh output displaces the summary; persistence is repaired by re-reading, so CL-W43-05's mechanism is not a reader failure for this agent and the lever is a re-read policy, which is the omission side C-W43-21 tests); or $u_F < 0.5\, u_S$ with non-overlapping bands (the agent discounts a value nothing ever produced, so provenance is partly consumed through plausibility and 'unsourced' is the less dangerous half of the summary, which contradicts the claim's noun). Protocol kill: fewer than 40 of 168 tasks meet the boundary-before-call condition, in which case the window is lowered to 2,048 tokens and the change reported, or the probe is parked if that fails too.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.45 for the claim as written: with the forced read, $u_S$ and $u_F$ in 0.35 to 0.60 and within 10 points of each other, $u_P$ 5 to 15 points above them (the agent executes its own stated decision more readily than a stated fact), $u_U = 0$; without the forced read the natural re-read rate is under 0.4 and uptake rises to 0.6 to 0.8. Conceded in advance: a frontier agent is a stronger reader than the paper's 7B, so uptake with the right value in view can fall under 0.25, which is the first kill and is itself the lane's first number on whether re-reading repairs a self-written summary.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: SJC reads its census (29 of 35 analyzed failures follow a summary entry; 22 of 29 failure-following entries unsupported, Table 11 after the 9-run exclusion, per CL-W43-05's record) as the agent treating every summary line as established, and gates on provenance; 2607.13071 names summaries inherited 'without re-verification'; the card paper shows a 7B reader picks the stale value in 41 of 74 matched-size swaps even under an explicit recency rule (Table 16); against these, 2305.13300 reports readers 'highly receptive to external evidence' when it is coherent, and 2606.25449 finds whether a lossy memory becomes a harmful action 'is a joint model-and-interface property', which predicts the fresh output wins for a strong agent.
preregistered_surprise.would_change: If the summary outranks the fresh output regardless of provenance: re-fetching cannot repair a compaction summary, only deleting or marking at the boundary can, the claim's 'unsourced persistence' is upgraded from a failure mode to one a re-read does not fix, and every compaction evaluation owes a contradiction-in-view cell beside its length and provenance numbers. If the fresh output wins: the fix is a re-read policy after compaction (the omission side), and provenance gates (SJC, C-W43-09) address a failure the agent repairs by itself when it looks. If $u_F \ll u_S$: the agent discounts values with no plausible origin, so unsourced entries are self-limiting and the dangerous entries are stale-but-sourced ones, which reverses the claim's noun.
preregistered_surprise.belief_changing: Either $u_S, u_F \geq 0.5$ with the right value in view (summary beats environment; re-read is not a fix) or $u_S, u_F \leq 0.25$ (environment beats summary; the mechanism is omission and re-read); a $u_F / u_S$ ratio under 0.5 changes the claim's noun either way.

title: Who moved in tau-bench 2.0: the user-simulator share of pass@1 variance at the leaderboard's one-trial protocol
statement: On the 150 English text-v1 tasks (airline, retail, telecom; the frozen 50-task frames), hold the agent at a non-reasoning model at temperature 0 (gpt-4.1-2025-04-14, the 1.x default) and run $K = 4$ trials in three user-simulator arms: (A) the 2.0 default, gpt-5.5 at reasoning_effort low, which has no temperature control; (B) the 1.x default, gpt-4.1 at temperature 0; (C) gpt-4.1 at temperature 1. Per task $t$ and arm $a$ compute the trial success rate $\hat p_{t,a}$ and the within-task outcome variance $V_{t,a} = \hat p_{t,a}(1 - \hat p_{t,a})$; arm B is the floor set by both parties' serving nondeterminism at temperature 0, so the user-simulator share of 2.0's trial-to-trial variance is $S_U = \overline{(V_{t,A} - V_{t,B})}\,/\,\overline{V_{t,A}}$ with the bar an average over tasks, and arm C calibrates $S_U$ against a user known to sample. From the saved `messages`, record for every mixed-outcome task the first turn index at which the four trials' transcripts differ and which party wrote it; from `review.errors[].source` and `review.critical_user_error` (fields in the log schema, null in every public trajectory opened on 2026-11-02), count critical user errors per arm. Report $S_U$ per domain beside the leaderboard's top-5 score gaps on the same frame.
claim: tau-bench 2.0 moved its user simulator to a reasoning model that cannot be pinned and cut the protocol to one trial, so the published pass@1 scores carry a user-simulator noise floor larger than the gaps they rank, and the benchmark's pass^k reads as user-draw consistency, not agent consistency.
trick: Run the same frozen agent several times against the benchmark's own simulated user, then against a pinned one, and measure how much of the score spread is the user rolling dice.
why_now: tau2-bench 2.0.0 (2026-10-19) changed the released-benchmark user simulator from gpt-4.1 at temperature 0 to openai/gpt-5.5 at reasoning_effort low and fixed the scored protocol at one trial (docs/running-the-benchmark.md: Trials (--num-trials) 1; docs/leaderboard-submission.md: 'The 2.0 benchmarks and voice-v1 are scored at one trial (pass@1). For 1.x text, at least 4 trials per domain are strongly preferred.'). The 1.x public trajectories (29 submission folders, about 40,000 objects in the public bucket on 2026-11-02; Sierra-run cells at 4 trials with a gpt-5.2 reasoning_effort-low user) already show per-call seeds and costs but every `review` field is null, so the user-error attribution the schema provides exists only on the owner's side. The flag: the identity $V = \hat p(1-\hat p)$ is old; the enabling piece is the protocol change, not a method.

killing_experiment.design: 1,800 calls: 150 tasks x 4 trials x 3 arms, agent gpt-4.1 at temperature 0 throughout, released text-v1 English cells, default judges (semantic communication judge gpt-5.5 low; NL-assertion judge gpt-5.4-mini low) held fixed. Compute $S_U$ per domain with a task-level bootstrap (resample tasks) for its interval; compute the first-divergence party for mixed-outcome tasks; run `tau2 judges` reviews on failed calls to fill `review.errors[].source`. Owner cost: at the public per-trajectory costs (agent about $0.40, user about $0.01 on the 4-trial Sierra runs), about $750 and two days at the default 3-call concurrency; the matrix runner resumes and shards by cell.
killing_experiment.kills_if: $S_U < 0.1$ in all three domains with the bootstrap interval excluding 0.3, and the first divergence is an agent turn in at least 80% of mixed-outcome tasks: the 2.0 user simulator adds no measurable outcome noise beyond the temperature-0 floor, the one-trial protocol is justified, and the result is a citable footnote that retires the 4-trial 1.x rule.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment p 0.5: $S_U \ge 0.3$ in airline and retail (where the tau2 paper's own annotators found 13% and 12% critical user errors with a temperature-0 gpt-4.1 user) and the first divergence is a user turn in a majority of mixed-outcome tasks; the task-level pass@1 spread across trials exceeds the leaderboard's top-5 gaps on the same frame.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: tau2-bench abstract: 'A reliable user simulator tightly coupled with the environment, whose behavior is constrained by tools and observable states, improving simulation fidelity'; tau-Voice: 'Error analysis attributes 79-90% of failures to agent behavior rather than simulator artifacts'; the 2.0 submission rule scores at one trial. The nearest outside work (2601.17087) reports a mean shift of up to 9 points across user LLMs, not a variance share at a fixed user.
preregistered_surprise.would_change: If $S_U \ge 0.3$: every 2.0 score needs a user-draw interval, pass^k on tau-bench is re-read as consistency over user draws rather than agent consistency, and the RL gym users get a per-domain reward-noise budget (CL-W44-J01's luck table on this environment). If $S_U < 0.1$: the one-trial protocol stands and the 4-trial rule can be dropped, cutting leaderboard cost by three quarters; the mean-shift finding of 2601.17087 is then a bias question, not a noise question.

identifiability: Random given: the task, the frozen frame and pins, the agent model at temperature 0 (its remaining variance is serving nondeterminism, measured by arm B), the user model and its sampling setting, the judge models and prompt versions saved with the run. The tau-bench environment is deterministic given the parties' messages and tool calls, so a trial-to-trial difference belongs to whichever party's text differs first; turns alternate, so the first-divergence party is well defined. $S_U$ is a property of (agent, user simulator, domain), not of the protocol, once arm B is subtracted; reasoning agents cannot be pinned and are excluded from the floor arm by construction. Judge noise is held fixed by using the same judge on all arms and is measured separately by re-scoring arm A with `tau2 evaluate-trajs` twice.
owner_only_field: the 2.0 matrix runner at K trials on the frozen frames; `review.errors[].source`, `review.critical_user_error`, `user_only_review` (schema fields, null in all public trajectories opened); the Sierra-internal voice IDs and the frozen 2026-10-02 voice-v2 release export; the persona block and `language-guidelines-v4` user prompts (public in the repo, but the reviewed labels are not).

adoption_surface: taubench.com (a user-draw interval column on the 2.0 tabs); the gym's RL users (a per-domain noise budget); tau-bench-derived benchmarks (J-tau 2610.19638, tau-Emotion 2610.19560, tau-Rec); HAL's reliability dashboard, which runs tau-bench airline with a gpt-4o user at provider-default sampling.
entry_ticket: Your 2.0 matrix can answer how much of a pass@1 score on the frozen 900-call frame is the simulated user's draw now that the user is gpt-5.5 at low reasoning effort and every cell is scored once. The obvious design, swap the user model and compare means, fails because it measures a bias between users (2601.17087 already shows up to 9 points) and not the noise a single user adds to one score. The identifiable design holds a non-reasoning agent at temperature 0 and runs four trials in three user arms, the 2.0 default, gpt-4.1 at temperature 0 as the floor, and gpt-4.1 at temperature 1 as the calibration, so the user share is the variance above the floor, with the first-divergence turn and your own `review.errors[].source` labels saying which party moved: 1,800 calls, about $750, two days. Pre-registered: we expect the user share above 0.3 in airline and retail and the per-task spread larger than your top-5 gaps; your papers assume the simulator is reliable and that 79-90% of failures are the agent's. Do you want it, and is anyone doing it?

title: Where HAL's five temperature-zero runs first diverge on tau-bench airline: the agent, the simulated user, or the stack
statement: HAL's reliability protocol runs each tau-bench airline task $K = 5$ times at agent temperature 0 and reads the spread as 'non-sampling sources of stochasticity'; its harness runs the original tau-bench with `user_model: gpt-4o` through a user simulator that passes no temperature argument, so the user samples at the provider default while the agent is pinned. From the owner's Weave traces (every user-simulator call is logged), align the five transcripts of each (model, task) cell turn by turn and record the first turn index $\tau^\ast$ at which any transcript differs and the party that wrote it (user turn, agent turn; tool results are deterministic functions of the agent's calls in tau-bench). Let $U$ be the share of mixed-outcome cells whose first divergence is a user turn. Then re-run three non-reasoning models x 26 tasks x 5 runs with the user pinned (temperature 0 and a fixed seed) and recompute the dashboard's outcome consistency $(2\hat p - 1)^2$ per task, reporting the change in each model's tau-bench consistency column and in the GAIA-versus-tau-bench ordering.
claim: A large share of the run-to-run inconsistency HAL reports on tau-bench at temperature 0 begins at a user-simulator turn, so the dashboard's tau-bench consistency column measures the simulated user plus the agent, and the serving-stack explanation applies to GAIA, not to tau-bench.
trick: Lay the five supposedly identical transcripts side by side, find the first word that differs, and see whether the agent or the fake customer wrote it.
why_now: The ICML version of the reliability paper (2602.16666 v3, 2026-06-02) and the dashboard's final results (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro and 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.7 added) fix the protocol: 'Each task is executed K=5 times with different random seeds... We set the temperature to zero so that any observed variance is attributable to non-sampling sources of stochasticity'. The harness file hal/benchmarks/taubench.py (archived repository, fetched 2026-11-02) sets `user_strategy: llm, user_model: gpt-4o` and the upstream tau-bench user simulator calls `completion(model=self.model, custom_llm_provider=self.provider, messages=messages)` with no temperature. The enabling piece is their own K = 5 traces; the analysis is a diff.

title: Is the tournament decided at warm-up? Rank persistence of Gambit's scorer and the one-shot control
statement: Gambit keeps $C = 256$ active traces and, every $\Delta = 200$ tokens after a warm-up of $w = 12{,}000$ tokens, prunes the bottom-$K$ and branches the top-$K$ ($K = 16$) by a hidden-state scorer. From the TraceTree logs of the published runs (three models x AIME-25, AIME-26, HMMT-24, HMMT-25, GPQA-Diamond), compute per problem the Spearman rank correlation $\rho_1$ between trace scores at the first check and at the last check among traces alive at both, and the share $\sigma$ of final completed traces whose founder lineage was in the top half at the first check. Then run the control the paper lacks: one swap at $w$ of size $K = C/2$ (prune the bottom half, branch the top half once) and no further tournaments, with the same capacity, scorer, warm-up, vote and GPU; 'one-shot'. Compare accuracy at matched completed traces ($N = 256$) and matched wall-clock, three seeds per cell.
claim: Gambit's accuracy gain over pruning is a single early selection plus full hardware utilization: the scorer's ranking at the first check already fixes the survivors, so a one-shot swap at warm-up matches the periodic tournament at the same capacity.
trick: Check whether the traces that win the final vote were already the top-ranked ones at the first checkpoint; if so, one early cut does the whole job.
why_now: Gambit v2 (2026-08-11) and its code release (vLLM v0.11.1 fork) are the first public tournament-style beam search with logged score histories; the paper's own ablation (Fig. 10) varies $\Delta$ in {100, 200, 400} and reads the smooth curve as robustness, which conflates selection timing with utilization. The flag: the rank-persistence statistic is old; the enabling piece is the logged tree.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 (owner, zero GPU-hours, one day): parse the saved TraceTrees; report $\rho_1$ and $\sigma$ per problem with their distribution per model and benchmark; also $\rho_k$ for every check $k$ to draw the persistence curve. Step 1 (owner, about 65 B300-hours, one week): the one-shot control on three models x AIME-25 and HMMT-24, three seeds each (the paper's runs are single); the paper's Table 3 gives about 38,000 s wall-clock per model-benchmark at $N = 256$, so six cells x three seeds is about 190 B300-hours at full length, reduced to about 65 by the one-shot arm's shorter tail. Report accuracy, unique tokens and wall-clock side by side with Gambit and STEP.
killing_experiment.kills_if: Median $\rho_1 < 0.3$ across problems and the one-shot control trails Gambit by more than 1 point on at least 4 of 6 cells at matched completed traces: the ranking is non-stationary along the trace and periodic re-selection is doing work; the paper's 'dynamically concentrates compute' stands with a measured persistence curve attached (citable either way).

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment p 0.5: median $\rho_1 \ge 0.7$, $\sigma \ge 0.8$, and the one-shot control is within 1 point of Gambit on at least 4 of 6 cells at matched traces, with lower wall-clock because the pool is refreshed once.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: Gambit: 'dynamically concentrates compute onto the most promising reasoning traces' and, on $\Delta = 400$, 'infrequent updates delay corrective selection'; STEP and DeepConf treat the score as a running filter. The motivation section already shows one branching event from the top prefix lifting pass@1 from 6.2% to 87.5% on one problem, which is the one-shot mechanism in miniature.
preregistered_surprise.would_change: If persistence is high: the default becomes a one-shot fork at warm-up, implementable with existing prefix-fork APIs in vLLM and SGLang without a tournament scheduler, and the hidden-state scorer's job is a single ranking; the design question moves to choosing $w$. If persistence is low: the scorer's signal changes along the trace, the history-aware sequence scorer (their A.1) becomes the live direction, and the tournament cadence $\Delta$ gets a principled setting from the persistence curve's decay.

identifiability: Ranks are a property of (model, scorer, problem, the paper's sampling settings) given the fork commit and the GPU; $\rho_1$ and $\sigma$ are computed on logged values with no new sampling. The one-shot control changes only the number and size of tournaments; capacity, scorer, warm-up, vote rule, hard floor and hardware are held fixed; three seeds per cell bound the sampling noise that the paper's single runs do not. Ghost traces (evicted but logically active) are handled as in the paper, and their count is logged so the comparison is at matched physical occupancy.
owner_only_field: the TraceTree score histories and topology of the published runs (the fork writes them; an outsider must compile the vLLM fork, 'sometimes several hours', and needs about 275 GB of KV for $C = 256$ at 35k tokens); the scheduler's eviction log; the per-model trained scorers; the B300.
first_measurement_cost_for_owner: zero GPU-hours and one day for the persistence statistics; about 65 B300-hours and one week for the one-shot control
adoption_surface: Gambit's defaults ($\Delta$, $w$); STEP and DeepConf successors; vLLM and SGLang maintainers deciding whether a tournament belongs in the scheduler or a one-shot fork suffices; anyone building parallel-thinking serving.
entry_ticket: Your trace trees can answer whether the tournament is decided at warm-up: if the traces that win the final vote were already top-ranked at the first check, one swap at $w$ does the whole job. The obvious design, ablate $\Delta$, fails because a longer interval changes utilization and selection together, which is why Fig. 10 reads as smooth. The identifiable design is the rank-persistence curve from your logs (zero GPU-hours) and a one-shot control, a single swap of size $C/2$ at warm-up with the same capacity, scorer and vote, three seeds on three models x two benchmarks (about 65 B300-hours). Pre-registered: we expect persistence above 0.7 and the one-shot arm within a point; your paper reads the gain as dynamic reallocation. Do you want it, and is anyone doing it?

title: How much of MuJoCo Warp's batched Newton solve is waiting for the slowest world: the per-world iteration distribution the nightly already records
statement: MJWarp's constraint solver iterates batch-wide: the loop `wp.capture_while(nsolving, ...)` runs the iteration kernels over all worlds until the count of unconverged worlds reaches zero ('it counts the number of worlds that are not converged, it becomes 0 when all worlds are converged'), and converged worlds return early inside kernels still launched over the full world dimension. The nightly suite runs `mjwarp-testspeed --measure_solver=true`, which records $n_{s,w}$, the iteration count of world $w$ at step $s$, for every step, and publishes only its mean and p95 (unitree_g1_flat: mean 3.01, p95 5; unitree_g1_hfield: 3.24, 6; aloha_clutter: 2.68, 6; three_humanoids: 2.67, 5; aloha_cloth: 34.3, 62; franka_emika_panda: 1.02, 1). Define the wait share $W = 1 - \frac{\sum_s \sum_w n_{s,w}}{\sum_s N \max_w n_{s,w}}$ with $N$ the world count: the fraction of launched world-iterations in which the world had already converged. Measure $W$, the per-step histogram of $n_{s,w}$, the share of worlds per step with $n_{s,w}$ at the cap (the `overflow & ITERATIONS` bit, which the unitree_g1 benchmark entries silence with `opt.warn_overflow=~ITERATIONS|~LS_ITERATIONS`; the G1 model ships `iterations="10" ls_iterations="20"`, 'derived from mjlab'), and the time `step.forward.solve` before and after a compacted launch over the unconverged-world index list on unitree_g1_hfield and three_humanoids.
claim: On the shipped RL configurations, MJWarp's batched Newton solve spends a large share of its launched work on worlds that have already converged, because the batch runs to the slowest world's iteration count while the median world stops at two or three; compacting the active-world list cuts the solve time by a margin the per-world distribution predicts.
trick: Count how many solver iterations each of the 8,192 worlds actually needed, compare with how many the batch ran, and the difference is the time the fast worlds spent waiting for the slow ones.
why_now: The nightly suite (first entries 2026-03-30) is the first public, continuous, per-scene log of solver iteration statistics for a GPU engine, and it already collects the per-world array it does not publish; the G1 benchmark model adopted mjlab's RL config (cap 10, line-search cap 20) and silences the cap-hit warning, so the shipped RL regime is on the nightly box. Newton's monthly cadence (1.7.0 on 2026-10-14) means a compacted launch lands within a release. The flag: the Amdahl argument is old; the enabling piece is the recorded array.

killing_experiment.design: Step 0 (owner, about 1 GPU-hour, one day): extend `--measure_solver` to write the per-step histogram of $n_{s,w}$, the active-world count per iteration launch, and the per-step cap-hit share from `d.overflow`; rerun the 18 scenes at their benchmark world counts with the replay controls; compute $W$ per scene and the Amdahl prediction of the solve-time saving, $1 - \frac{\sum_s \overline{n_s}}{\sum_s \max_w n_{s,w}}$ with $\overline{n_s}$ the mean over worlds, under the assumption that launch cost is proportional to launched worlds. Step 1 (owner, about one engineer-week): a prototype that launches the iteration kernels over a compacted index list of unconverged worlds (rebuilt each iteration from `ctx.done`), bit-for-bit state comparison against the current loop after 1,000 steps, and `step.forward.solve` before and after on unitree_g1_hfield (solve 218 of 590 ns per step on the nightly box) and three_humanoids (626 of 915 ns).
killing_experiment.kills_if: $W < 0.15$ on every locomotion and manipulation scene (the per-world distribution is thin: p99 within one iteration of the mean) and the compacted launch changes `step.forward.solve` by less than 10%: iteration-level scheduling is dead on MJWarp at these world counts, L5's kill test #2 fails, and the lane's systems piece is retired with a measured reason.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment p 0.5: $W \ge 0.4$ on unitree_g1_hfield and aloha_clutter (the batch runs to a p99 of 7-10 while the median world stops at 2-3), the cap of 10 is hit by 0.5-3% of worlds per step on the G1 scenes (the silenced warning), and the compacted launch cuts solve time by at least 30%, which is at least 10% of step time on the G1 scenes and about 20% on three_humanoids.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: MJWarp docs (fetched 2026-11-02): 'With MJWarp, in contrast, once all worlds have converged the solver can early exit and avoid unnecessary computation. As a result, the values of these settings have comparatively less impact on performance', and 'Reducing these limits too much may prevent the constraint solver from converging and can lead to inaccurate or unstable simulation'; the batch-level view of early exit. GPUSimBench (2607.13059) reports throughput, memory and determinism without per-world iteration data.
preregistered_surprise.would_change: If $W \ge 0.4$: the nightly page gains two columns (wait share, cap-hit share), compaction becomes a Newton change, and RL configs get a measured population of capped steps on which CL-W43-01's per-step audit runs first. If $W < 0.15$: the scheduler idea is retired on this engine, which also says the cap of 10 is rarely binding on locomotion and moves CL-W43-01's attention to contact-rich manipulation (aloha_clutter, aloha_cloth, where p95 is 6 and 62).

identifiability: $n_{s,w}$ is a property of (scene, control replay, world count, cap, tolerance, GPU, commit), all fixed by the benchmark entry; the replay files (e.g. shuffle_dance.npz) make the distribution reproducible up to GPU-batch nondeterminism, which Newton's `deterministic` option removes at a throughput cost that is itself reported. $W$ is a deterministic function of the recorded counts under a stated launch-cost model, and the compaction prototype changes launch structure only, not arithmetic, so a step-by-step state comparison is the correctness check; any state difference is a bug, not a result. `converged_worlds` in the nightly counts worlds without NaN positions and is not a convergence certificate; the certificate at exit (the gradient test in `_solve_done`) lives in the solver context and is not exported, which is other_questions[0].
owner_only_field: the per-world `solver_niter` arrays per step on the nightly box (collected by `--measure_solver`, published as mean and p95 only); the per-world `overflow & ITERATIONS` flags (silenced in the G1 entries); the replay controls; and the iteration loop itself, which only the maintainers can restructure without a fork.
first_measurement_cost_for_owner: about 1 GPU-hour and one day for the histogram and wait share; about one engineer-week for the compacted-launch prototype
adoption_surface: the MJWarp nightly page (two columns); Newton's SolverMuJoCo; mjlab, Isaac Lab (Newton branch) and MuJoCo Playground configs choosing `iterations`; RL groups reporting solver settings.
entry_ticket: Your nightly already records how many Newton iterations each of the 8,192 worlds needed per step and publishes the mean and p95; it can answer how much of `step.forward.solve` is launched work on worlds that had already converged, because the loop runs until the last world is done. The obvious design, lower the iteration cap and time it, fails because it changes the physics and the waiting at once, which is why the docs can say the setting has little effect. The identifiable design is the wait share from the recorded per-world counts, the cap-hit share from the overflow bit your G1 entries silence, and a compacted launch over the unconverged-world list checked bit-for-bit against the current loop: about one GPU-hour for the numbers, a week for the prototype. Pre-registered: we expect a wait share above 0.4 on g1_hfield and aloha_clutter and a 30% cut in solve time; the docs read early exit as batch-wide. Do you want it, and is anyone doing it?

scorecard.target_value: Asked in print: the MJWarp docs' performance-tuning page (the iteration settings are 'secondary considerations'); the G1 benchmark's own override silencing the cap warnings; GPUSimBench's call that 'the underlying trade-offs between parallel efficiency, physical fidelity, and execution determinism remain largely unexamined'. Who pays: every group training policies in MJWarp or Newton at thousands of worlds, and the engine teams choosing defaults (Newton ships 100 / 50; mjlab's G1 ships 10 / 20).

impact_ceiling.floor: A wait-share and cap-hit table across the 18 nightly scenes; two columns on the nightly page. Requires 1 GPU-hour. Judgment p 0.5.
impact_ceiling.middle: A compacted-launch change in Newton's SolverMuJoCo with a measured 10-20% step-time gain on locomotion scenes, and RL configs reporting cap-hit share. Requires the prototype and review. Judgment p 0.3.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The first measured population of capped steps on shipped RL configs feeding CL-W43-01's exploit audit, with the fidelity-throughput frontier drawn per scene (the L5 lane's measurement headline). Requires the 2x2 training arm (P-W43-01-2x2). Judgment p 0.15.

Systems route (Lloyd/Netravali): the scheduler is GPU scheduling. scorecard.density_and_ownership: arXiv API 2026-11-02: '(solver iterations) AND (batched OR parallel worlds OR GPU) AND (physics OR simulator) AND (straggler OR slowest OR early exit OR load imbalance) AND (robot OR contact)' = 0; 'GPU AND (physics engine OR rigid body) AND (batched OR parallel environments OR worlds) AND (load balancing OR straggler OR early exit OR scheduling) AND (solver OR contact)' = 0; '(solver iterations OR iteration cap OR solver budget) AND (reinforcement learning OR policy) AND (sim-to-real OR transfer OR exploit) AND (MuJoCo OR Isaac OR physics engine)' = 0; '(physics engine OR simulator) AND benchmark AND (accuracy OR fidelity) AND (speed OR throughput) AND GPU' = 3 (GPUPhysBench 2609.35639: correctness as matching expert code; ComFree-Sim 2603.12185: an analytical contact engine; one unrelated). Nearest with their words: GPUSimBench 2607.13059 ('significant run-to-run and inter-environment variability even under identical initial conditions'; no iteration data); mjlab 2601.22074 (the source of the cap-10 G1 config; no solver statistics in its abstract); Isaac Lab 2511.04831. Owner: the docs' tuning page and the nightly's mean/p95 columns. Not published: per-world iteration distributions, a wait share, or a cap-hit share on any scene. Race window: the GPU-simulator measurement lane produced two meta-benchmarks in 2026 (GPUSimBench, GPUPhysBench); time to result one day for the numbers from the owner's position.
scorecard.why_now: Nightly suite with `--measure_solver` since 2026-03-30; G1 benchmark on mjlab's RL config with the cap warnings silenced; Newton 1.7.0 (2026-10-14) with a `deterministic` option that makes the bit-for-bit check possible.

other_questions.q: Which worlds hit the cap, and what is their physics? Export the solver's exit certificate (the gradient and improvement tests in `_solve_done`) per world beside `solver_niter`, and on the G1 scenes relate cap-hit steps to contact count, `nefc` and foot-impact phase; then re-simulate those steps at cap 100 to measure the one-step state error concentrated on capped steps.

other_questions.surprise: ours: capped steps cluster at impacts and carry most of the one-step error between cap 10 and cap 100, so the RL config's inaccuracy lives in under 5% of steps; theirs: 'reducing these limits too much may prevent the constraint solver from converging' as a global warning; belief-changing: the per-step audit of CL-W43-01 gets its population, and a per-world adaptive cap becomes the obvious design.

other_questions.q: Forward-inverse consistency on the GPU: MuJoCo CPU's `solver_fwdinv` residual is the standard self-check of a constraint solve; MJWarp's types.py lists FWDINV as unsupported ('# unsupported: OVERRIDE, FWDINV, ISLAND, DIAGEXACT'). Implement the batched residual and publish it per scene on the nightly.

other_questions.first_measurement: engineer-days to implement; about 1 GPU-hour to run across scenes
other_questions.surprise: ours: the fwdinv residual tracks the cap-hit share and nothing in throughput, giving the nightly a fidelity column that moves independently of speed; theirs: the nightly tracks speed and memory only; belief-changing: a numbers-only fidelity score exists per commit (CL-W43-J03's question of which such numbers predict transfer gets a candidate).

other_questions.q: The batch-nondeterminism floor per scene: run each nightly scene twice with identical seeds, with and without Newton's `deterministic` option, and report the per-world state divergence after 1,000 steps and the throughput cost of determinism; the twin of CL-W43-09's resolution floor.
other_questions.owner_only: owner-cheap rather than owner-only: anyone with an NVIDIA GPU can run it; the owner has the box, the replay controls and the release process to publish it per commit.
other_questions.surprise: ours: determinism costs under 10% on locomotion scenes and the divergence without it exceeds the policy-return differences robot-RL papers report as improvements; theirs: Newton's changelog treats determinism as an opt-in for debugging; belief-changing: determinism becomes the default for evaluation runs and a reported column.
other_questions.adoption: Newton defaults; RL papers' evaluation protocol.

other_questions.q: The nightly history as a physics-regression log (solo-doable, not owner-only): 250 nights x 18 scenes of solver_niter_mean and p95 against commit; find commits that shifted a scene's iteration distribution by more than 20% while the speed chart read as a win or no change.
