reopen_trigger: lab compute of >= 3500 GPU-hours and a shared harness (one open scaffold with a pluggable compaction hook and the paired-continuation instrument)
title: Damage versus dose: the compute-matched, dose-matched comparison of compaction recipes under a forced window, with random deletion as the floor
statement: Run 13 published compaction recipes, the production default and the two cheap incumbents (tool-result clearing, truncation) in one open harness under a hard $64\,\text{K}$ window on tasks that must compact at least twice, at the same retained-token fraction $r$ and the same uncached-prefill budget, against random deletion at the same $r$, a wrong-task placebo summary and a shuffled summary, on SWE-bench Verified, Terminal-Bench 2.0 and a side-constraint set where the lost information is not on disk; report damage $D = 1 - s_{\text{arm}}/s_{\text{ref}}$ against $r$ by pass-rate band.
claim: Once retained tokens and uncached prefill are matched and a random-deletion floor is drawn, the published compaction recipes for coding agents separate into two bands, mechanical-reversible and model-written, and the model-written band does not beat random deletion on compaction-friendly benchmarks; only the side-constraint set separates recipes.
trick: Make every recipe keep the same number of tokens and spend the same prefill, then see which ones still beat deleting at random.
why_now: The instrument (paired continuation, Compact-Bench 2026-10-22), the control (random deletion at matched budget, 2610.27301 2026-10-19) and the harness with hooks (2610.31778 2026-10-22) all landed within five weeks; the lane published 11 compaction papers in the two weeks to 2026-10-28 and none of them is compute- or dose-matched against the others.

killing_experiment.design: Pilot of the forced regime only: 2 recipes (self-summary, TRC) plus random deletion at $r = 0.25$ on 60 qualifying SWE-bench tasks, 3 seeds, one 27B model, under the $64\,\text{K}$ cap, with the paired-continuation readout.
killing_experiment.kills_if: Random deletion is more than 10 points below both recipes on the paired readout with non-overlapping bootstrap bands in the middle pass-rate band: the floor is not a floor, the field's assumption holds, and the comparison is a service rather than a paper (the spec still stands as a service spec).

spec.problem: Which context-compaction recipe should a long-horizon coding agent run, at what retained-token dose, and does any published recipe beat deleting at random once dose and compute are matched?

recipes.name: self-summarization (production default; OpenCode/Claude Code/Codex prompt)
recipes.trick: When the window fills, ask the same model to write a summary of its work and restart from the summary.

recipes.name: tool-result clearing (TRC; Anthropic clear_tool_uses)
recipes.trick: Replace old tool outputs with a placeholder and keep everything else verbatim; no model call.

recipes.name: truncation (oldest-first)
recipes.trick: Drop the oldest messages until the target size is reached; keeps the recent trajectory verbatim.

recipes.name: ReFold
recipes.trick: Keep the full history but render stubs for content an earlier turn already displayed and one-line notes for turns the agent itself declared finished; reversible, no model call.

recipes.name: SJC (source-judged compaction)
recipes.trick: After the summary is written, score each entry for whether an environment output or the previous summary supports it, and delete the unsupported entries.

recipes.name: FOCUS (decision-preserving compression)
recipes.trick: At test time, keep the past interaction units whose removal would change the agent's next decision and drop the rest.

recipes.name: ACON (optimized compression guidelines; pre-window precedent)
recipes.trick: Iteratively rewrite the compression prompt's guidelines from failure analyses of the agent, in natural language, no parameter updates.

recipes.name: CliffCompaction
recipes.trick: Compact by truncating only what can be dropped faithfully, so the compacted record never asserts what the history does not contain; cuts cost up to 50% under a bounded window.

recipes.name: CADOC
recipes.trick: Replace structured objects in the history with small retrieval cards, batching the replacements by an economic-order-quantity rule so prefix-cache reuse is not broken at every turn.

recipes.name: CCM (continuous context management)
recipes.trick: Compact at every turn: the agent emits an updated memory with each action and the next prompt is task + memory + newest observation.

recipes.name: StateComp (learned when-to-compress router)
recipes.trick: Train a router on the frozen model's hidden states to label past interactions KEEP or READY-to-replace given the current agent state.

recipes.name: AutoCompact (RL-trained compaction policy)
recipes.trick: Make when-to-compact, what-to-keep and how-to-continue part of the agent's policy, trained by judge-corrected SFT then RL on task success.

recipes.name: transparent-compact
recipes.trick: Deterministic compaction that leaves user and assistant prose unchanged and marks exactly where information was stripped.

recipes.name: filesystem offloading
recipes.trick: Write the full history to a JSON file before summarizing and tell the summary where it is, so nothing is unrecoverable.

recipes.name: random deletion at matched budget
recipes.trick: Delete sentences (or words) at random to the same token budget; the control every compaction method must beat.

recipes.name: Compact-Bench paired continuation
recipes.trick: Continue the same repository state once from the full history and once from the summary, and count repairs that only the full history completes.

recipes.name: CONPACT side-constraint suite
recipes.trick: Inject a user rule such as 'do not delete emails until I confirm', compact, and measure whether the rule survives and is obeyed.

recipes.name: REMORY
recipes.trick: Append learned soft memory tokens after the summary so a frozen model's continuation approximates the full-history continuation.

recipes.name: LOHA + ACD
recipes.trick: Compress old tool observations into soft tokens while keeping the agent's own turns and the last K observations as text; distil to keep behaviour anchored.

recipes.name: CTXAgent (self-controlled context)
recipes.trick: Give the model two context tools and one paragraph of guidance and let it decide when to compact, what to keep and what to hand off.

recipes.name: Bud ContextCompact 2.0
recipes.trick: Runtime compaction tuned for small models and small windows; raises a 27B model's resolve rate on long SWE-bench sessions at a 49K window.

recipes.name: AgentFold (pre-window precedent)
recipes.trick: Learn a per-step 'fold' operation that condenses history at several scales instead of appending raw observations.

recipes.name: FoldAct
recipes.trick: Treat summary actions as changing the observation space and train them with their own stabilised signal so RL with folding does not collapse.

spec.harness: One open harness with a pluggable compaction hook: the OpenCode fork released with 2610.31778 (its five strategies are already hooks) or mini-swe-agent as in 2609.32961; every recipe is implemented as a replacement for the hook and nothing else changes (tools, prompts, retry logic). Models served locally with vLLM, prefix caching on, so uncached prefill is measured, not estimated.

regime.forced_window: A hard context cap $W = 64\,\text{K}$ tokens for every arm (assumption: small enough that the tasks below compact at least twice; 2609.32961 saw fewer than 2 compactions per SWE-bench run at calibrated thresholds, which is why its comparison is not forced).
regime.task_selection: Only tasks whose uncompacted trajectory reaches peak context $\geq 2.5\,W$ in a pilot at a 1M window (assumption: about 40% of SWE-bench Verified and 60% of Terminal-Bench 2.0 tasks qualify for a 35B model; the pilot sets the number).
regime.benchmarks: SWE-bench Verified long-trajectory subset (target 150 tasks), Terminal-Bench 2.0 (target 60 tasks), and one non-compaction-friendly set where the constraint is not on disk: the CONPACT long-horizon research scenario (2608.11242) with injected side constraints (target 100 sessions). 2610.31778's own text: current benchmarks are compaction-friendly because progress stays on disk; a definitive table needs one set where it does not.
regime.model_band: Open weights 27B to 35B active-or-total (Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Qwen3.8-27B, both used by the closest papers), with one frontier API model on a 30-task subset as a transfer check (not compute-matched; reported separately).

spec.matched_compute: Per task a fixed budget of uncached prefill tokens $P$ and model calls $C$ (assumption: $P = 3\,\text{M}$, $C = 80$; set from the full-context pilot's 75th percentile). A run that exhausts either is scored as failed. Wall-clock and GPU-seconds are logged per run on the same engine so cost is measured, not derived from a price list (2609.32961 assumed a 10:1 cached price ratio; this spec measures prefill).
spec.matched_dose: Every arm compacts at the same boundaries (the forced window cap) to the same retained budget $r\,W$ with $r \in \{0.15, 0.25, 0.40\}$ (assumption: 0.25 is the common scaffold default; the other two bracket it). Dose is the retained-token fraction $r$ and the number of boundaries $n_b$. Learned triggers (AutoCompact, StateComp) and every-turn recipes (CCM) get a second arm with a free trigger but the same total retained tokens over the run, so a gain that comes from compacting more often or less deeply is separated from a gain in what is kept.
controls: Random deletion at the same $r$ (2610.27301's control), sentence-level and word-level.
Placebo summary: a summary of the same length written for a different task from the same benchmark, inserted at the same boundary (the wrong-task placebo for any claim that content matters).
Shuffled summary: the arm's own summary with its entries permuted (tests order and provenance claims such as SJC's).
No-compaction reference at a 1M window on the same tasks (the ceiling that defines damage).
Pass-rate bands: tasks binned by the no-compaction reference's pass rate over 3 seeds into $[0, 0.2)$, $[0.2, 0.8)$, $[0.8, 1]$; every number reported by band.
Entropy-only version: keep the $r\,W$ tokens with the highest next-token entropy under the policy (the content-free selector that several recipes may collapse to).
metrics: Damage fraction $D = 1 - s_{\text{arm}} / s_{\text{ref}}$ where $s$ is the pass rate over 3 seeds and the reference is the 1M-window run (paired by task).
Paired damage and rescue from the same pre-boundary state (Compact-Bench protocol): continue once from the full history and once from the compacted context.
Side-constraint retention and compliance (CONPACT protocol) on the research-scenario set.
Uncached prefill tokens, calls, GPU-seconds per run; prefix-cache hit rate.
spec.single_plot: Damage $D$ against dose $r$ at the forced window, one curve per recipe with its 95% task-bootstrap band, the random-deletion curve drawn as the floor and the TRC curve as the cheap incumbent, one panel per benchmark (the third panel is the side-constraint set). A recipe whose curve lies inside the random-deletion band on a panel is dead on that panel.

preregistered_expectation.expected: Judgment probability 0.55. On SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench the summarization family (self-summary, ACON, SJC, FOCUS, transparent-compact, CliffCompaction) collapses to one band within 3 points of each other at every $r$; TRC and ReFold sit on or above that band at lower uncached prefill; random deletion is within 5 points of the summarization band at $r = 0.25$ on SWE-bench (the compaction-friendly case) and 15 or more points below it on the side-constraint set; the learned triggers' published gains shrink below 3 points once total retained tokens are matched (their gain was dose, not policy).
preregistered_expectation.field_assumes: That a model-written summary beats mechanical deletion and that a better summarizer or a learned trigger is the lever. 2609.32961 already reports TRC matching full-context success at 0.57x tokens on SWE-bench while summarization loses 11 points; 2610.31778 reports no strategy beating default self-summarization; 2610.27301 reports no current-question sentence selector beating random deletion on later questions.
preregistered_expectation.would_change: If the expected result holds: every compaction paper reports damage-versus-dose with the random-deletion floor; harness defaults move to TRC-plus-reversible-stubs with summaries only for the side-constraint layer; cost teams stop pricing compaction by tokens saved. If a recipe beats random deletion by more than 10 points on every panel at matched dose and compute: that recipe becomes the default and the question moves to why its selection rule works.

breakdown: Main grid: 16 arms (13 recipes + 3 controls) x 310 tasks x 3 seeds x 2 models = 29,760 runs at $r = 0.25$.
Dose sweep: 7 arms x 2 extra $r$ values x 100 tasks x 3 seeds x 2 models = 8,400 runs.
Reference and pilot: 310 tasks x 3 seeds x 2 models at a 1M window = 1,860 runs.
Learned arms: fine-tuning AutoCompact and StateComp routers on the chosen harness: 300 GPU-hours (assumption: their papers' recipes at 27B scale).
assumptions: 0.08 GPU-hours per agent run: a 35B-A3B or 27B model on H100s under vLLM with prefix caching, 60 to 80 calls, mean prompt 40K tokens, 30K decode tokens; the pilot measures this and rescales the grid.
40,000 runs x 0.08 = 3,200 GPU-hours, plus 450 for learned arms and scoring; the range is 2,000 to 7,000 if the per-run cost is off by 2x.

consumers: Every compaction and context-management paper (Gate 3 community-wide): report damage-versus-dose against the random-deletion floor and TRC on the shared harness, or the comparison is not accepted.
Harness builders (OpenCode, OpenHands, Claude Code, Codex, Pi): the default trigger, retained fraction and primitive.
Serving and cost teams: whether compaction is priced by uncached prefill rather than tokens saved (2610.34763 shows the sign can flip).
RL trainers putting compaction in the loop (CompactionRL 2607.05378, KV-streams 2609.35750, FoldAct): which primitive to train against.
Benchmark owners: a side-constraint track becomes part of agent benchmarks because the compaction-friendly ones cannot separate recipes.
spec.why_not_run: Each recipe paper evaluates on its own harness, benchmark and model against self-summarization only, with the recipe's own trigger (dose unmatched). The two systematic studies used harness primitives, not published recipes: implementing a recipe in someone else's harness is weeks of work per recipe and 2609.32961 needed 35,000 runs for 12 primitives. Frontier labs run the comparison on their own models (2610.31778 cites DeepSeek-V3.2 section 4.4 and Kimi K2.5 section 5.2) and do not release the harness. The random-deletion control is three weeks old (2610.27301, 2026-10-19), and the forced-regime design needs tasks long enough to compact twice, which are the expensive ones. No single author of a recipe is paid to show it ties random deletion.
spec.enabling_piece: Three pieces landed in five weeks: the paired-continuation protocol with released data (Compact-Bench, 2026-10-22), the random-deletion-at-matched-budget control (2610.27301, 2026-10-19), and an open harness with five compaction hooks and code (2610.31778, 2026-10-22). Before October 2026 there was no shared instrument that isolates one compaction event.

closest_comparisons.title: Benchmarks Are Surprisingly Compaction-Friendly
closest_comparisons.what_it_has: One scaffold (OpenCode), five compaction strategies implemented as hooks, four frontier models, three long-horizon benchmarks (PaperBench 3 papers, ProgramBench 2 tasks, PostTrainBench 2 models x 3 targets), thresholds 160K-380K, two runs per task-configuration, bootstrap CIs.
closest_comparisons.lacks: No published recipe (its five arms are self-summary, tool-output pruning, filesystem offload, reasoning-block discard, small-model summary); no matched dose (thresholds 'are not comparable across models because compaction frequency depends on how fast each model's context grows', its own words); no matched compute (accuracy conditional on a valid submission, no prefill or wall-clock in the result); no random-deletion or placebo control; closed models only, two runs per cell, three to six tasks per benchmark; its own limitation text: 'four models, three benchmarks and a few tasks per each benchmark due to cost and compute constraints. We fix one scaffold'.

closest_comparisons.title: Beyond Token Savings: A Systematic Study of Context Compression in LLM Agents
closest_comparisons.what_it_has: Twelve harness primitives decomposed into primitive x trigger x depth, mini-swe-agent, three open-weight models, 100 SWE-bench Verified issues (three repos) and 40 Terminal-Bench 1.0 tasks, three runs per cell, about 35,000 runs, measured latency and estimated billed cost, task-level gains and losses.
closest_comparisons.lacks: No published recipe (no ACON, SJC, FOCUS, ReFold, CADOC, StateComp, AutoCompact); not a forced regime (thresholds at the 5th to 25th percentile of uncompacted peak context, so most trajectories compact fewer than twice on SWE-bench); dose differs by policy (step-triggered arms compact after every step); billed cost assumed at a 10:1 cached ratio rather than measured; no random-deletion or placebo control; no pass-rate bands; models no larger than 35B-A3B; its related-work section positions it against serving characterizations, not against the recipe literature.

closest_comparisons.title: Compact-Bench (third-closest)
closest_comparisons.what_it_has: Paired full-history versus summary-only continuations from one repository state across 14 summarizer backbones and 5 production prompts; recurring-detail retention on 146 real sessions; 224 production boundaries.
closest_comparisons.lacks: Only the summarizer backbone and prompt vary (no deletion, stub, learned-trigger or every-turn arms); 35 small repairs with an eight-step continuation; a measurement of one compaction event, not of a run under a forced window; no cost axis.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.55. On SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench the summarization family (self-summary, ACON, SJC, FOCUS, transparent-compact, CliffCompaction) collapses to one band within 3 points of each other at every $r$; TRC and ReFold sit on or above that band at lower uncached prefill; random deletion is within 5 points of the summarization band at $r = 0.25$ on SWE-bench (the compaction-friendly case) and 15 or more points below it on the side-constraint set; the learned triggers' published gains shrink below 3 points once total retained tokens are matched (their gain was dose, not policy).
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: That a model-written summary beats mechanical deletion and that a better summarizer or a learned trigger is the lever. 2609.32961 already reports TRC matching full-context success at 0.57x tokens on SWE-bench while summarization loses 11 points; 2610.31778 reports no strategy beating default self-summarization; 2610.27301 reports no current-question sentence selector beating random deletion on later questions.
preregistered_surprise.would_change: If the expected result holds: every compaction paper reports damage-versus-dose with the random-deletion floor; harness defaults move to TRC-plus-reversible-stubs with summaries only for the side-constraint layer; cost teams stop pricing compaction by tokens saved. If a recipe beats random deletion by more than 10 points on every panel at matched dose and compute: that recipe becomes the default and the question moves to why its selection rule works.

identifiability: Random given: one harness, one served model at a stated temperature, one task at a pinned image, one seed; the environment (a container) is deterministic after the action, so run-to-run variance is the policy's sampling. Damage $D$ is a property of (recipe, $r$, $W$, model, benchmark); the reference is the same tasks at a 1M window. Pass-rate bands are defined from the reference's three seeds. The side-constraint set's compliance score is a verifier (a rule either held or not), not a judge.

reopen_trigger: lab compute of >= 14000 GPU-hours and a shared harness (one verl-based stack with the recipes as plug-in estimators and one forkable long-horizon environment)
title: Credit at matched compute: the definitive comparison of step-credit and critic recipes for long-horizon agent RL against large flat groups and shuffled credit
statement: Re-implement 14 published step-credit and critic recipes as plug-in advantage estimators on one verl stack with one actor loss, train each on ALFWorld, WebShop and one forkable long-horizon environment with Qwen3-8B and Qwen2.5-7B at a fixed sampled-token budget $T$ that charges branches, siblings, critic passes and judge calls, with a fixed dose of non-zero-advantage tokens, against flat GRPO at group 8 and group 32, each recipe's shuffled credit, a placebo critic and an entropy-only targeting rule; report success at $T$, $0.5\,T$ and $2\,T$ by pass-rate band and plot the gain against the environment's measured decision density $\rho$.
claim: At matched rollout compute, a large flat GRPO group absorbs most of the published gain of critic-free step-credit recipes on the standard agent benchmarks, those recipes do not beat their own shuffled credit in the first two thirds of a trajectory, and only stabilized critics and counterfactual branching keep a gain, and only where decision density is low.
trick: Give every credit recipe the same number of sampled tokens, including its branches and its critic, and let a bigger flat group and a shuffled copy of the recipe's own weights compete with it.
why_now: verl with four credit methods already re-implemented (2026-05), decision density as a measurable property (2026-06), forkable environments for counterfactual credit (2026-09) and twin-world noise keying (2026-10) make the credit-quality ground truth and the shared stack available; the lane published 22 credit papers in October 2026 alone, none compute-matched against another.

killing_experiment.design: Pilot on ALFWorld only with Qwen2.5-7B: flat GRPO group 8, flat GRPO group 32 at the same token budget, GiGPO, and GiGPO with shuffled step credit, 3 seeds each, 300 optimizer steps, plus the credit-quality readout at 200 decision points.
killing_experiment.kills_if: GiGPO beats both group-32 GRPO and its shuffled control by more than 5 points with non-overlapping 3-seed bands in the middle pass-rate band, and its step advantage correlates with the counterfactual return difference above 0.3 in the first two thirds: the cheap incumbent and the shuffled control do not absorb the gain, CL-W43-06 is refuted on its own benchmark, and the comparison's expected result is the field's assumption (service, not paper).

spec.problem: At matched rollout compute and matched gradient dose, which step-credit and critic recipes for long-horizon agent RL beat flat GRPO, beat a large flat group, and beat their own shuffled credit, and in which horizon and pass-rate band?

recipes.name: flat GRPO, group of 8 (production default; pre-window)
recipes.trick: Normalize the trajectory reward within a group of rollouts of the same prompt and give every token that one advantage.

recipes.name: GiGPO (pre-window precedent)
recipes.trick: Group steps across the trajectories by matching anchor states and compute a second, step-level relative advantage at each matched state; critic-free.

recipes.name: Turn-PPO
recipes.trick: PPO with a learned critic whose advantage is estimated per turn instead of per token; found more robust than GRPO on multi-turn tasks.

recipes.name: EasyPPO
recipes.trick: Keep the critic trained on truncated rollouts too and weight each prompt's critic loss by the inverse spread of its returns, so the critic stops destabilizing PPO.

recipes.name: Odysseus PPO with a lightweight turn-level critic
recipes.trick: Replace the large token-level value model by a small turn-level critic (a CNN on the game frame) and clip negative advantages; beats GRPO and Reinforce++ on a 100-turn game.

recipes.name: LVRL
recipes.trick: Ask a frozen LLM, conditioned on the group's rollouts and calibrated at the known start and end values, for state values, and use value differences as step credit.

recipes.name: FOCUS (active critic)
recipes.trick: Branch continuations from the states where the critic is most uncertain, use the branches as critic targets, and score segments with a TD($\lambda$) advantage.

recipes.name: SCALE
recipes.trick: Have the critic predict the probability of eventual success at each prefix as well as the return, and turn changes in that probability into multi-step credit.

recipes.name: CRR (counterfactual rollout replay)
recipes.trick: At a few decision points, restore the container state, sample one alternative action, roll it forward, and replace the step advantage by the difference in terminal return.

recipes.name: TWICE (twin-world credit)
recipes.trick: Key every token's sampling noise by turn and line so a counterfactual branch inherits the factual episode's downstream luck; paired return differences become turn advantages.

recipes.name: trajectory-graph step advantages
recipes.trick: Merge the group's trajectories into a graph of shared states so the mean return of the actions leaving a state estimates its value without extra sampling.

recipes.name: GraphHCA
recipes.trick: Compute the hindsight-to-behaviour probability ratio in closed form on the rollout graph instead of training a hindsight model.

recipes.name: SCOPE
recipes.trick: Let the policy write hindsight skills for its own failed steps and distil them only at those steps, with a bounded signed coefficient.

recipes.name: SHARPO
recipes.trick: Reweight GRPO advantages per environment-facing segment by a teacher-student log-probability gap from privileged self-distillation.

recipes.name: ProAS
recipes.trick: Shape the uniform advantage by a progress estimate so structurally unreasonable actions in winning trajectories are not reinforced.

recipes.name: T2SPO
recipes.trick: Derive remaining-distance targets from past successful trajectories and pay each step by its progress toward them.

recipes.name: progress advantage
recipes.trick: Use the log-probability ratio between the RL-trained policy and its reference policy as a free step-level advantage; no reward model.

recipes.name: GACA
recipes.trick: Mix episode-level and step-level credit per decision by a criticality score from the response's normalized negative log-likelihood.

recipes.name: ECPO
recipes.trick: Shrink GiGPO's step credit at anchor states with few samples and gate it by within-action variance, against lucky-action bias.

recipes.name: CCPO
recipes.trick: Weight observation-matched peers by context similarity and discount detours inside successful trajectories.

recipes.name: ProVer
recipes.trick: An agentic judge contrasts a group's successes and failures to propose the pivotal segment, which then gets the credit.

recipes.name: ABSeeker (ABC)
recipes.trick: Backtrack from the final answer through the evidence chain and pay the steps on it.

recipes.name: VETTA
recipes.trick: Learn turn-level and token-level credit jointly and coordinate them in one update.

recipes.name: decision density (instrument)
recipes.trick: Define the fraction $\rho$ of turns whose action changes the return distribution; trajectory-level estimators lose signal-to-noise as $\rho^{-1/2}$.

recipes.name: CRAFT
recipes.trick: Counterfactual token importance from free sibling rollouts replaces the single scalar gate of self-distillation.

recipes.name: SGCD
recipes.trick: Use sibling-rollout contrast summarised by an external model as a bounded credit weight on the policy gradient, not as a competing loss.

spec.harness: One RL stack (verl, in which 2605.27881 re-implemented four credit methods and in which GiGPO's lineage lives), one rollout engine (vLLM), one environment interface. Every recipe is a plug-in advantage estimator or critic on the same actor loss with the same clipping, the same KL setting and the same sampling temperature; the authors' released code is used to check each re-implementation reproduces the published number on its own benchmark before it enters the table.

regime.environments: Three, chosen for horizon: ALFWorld (the lane's consensus benchmark, 10 to 30 turns), WebShop (5 to 15 turns), and one long-horizon executable one with forkable state so counterfactual recipes can run: AppWorld or a Terminal-Bench training split (30 to 100 turns). Assumption: the long one is the only place the field claims critics are needed (Odysseus, 2606.22164).
regime.forced_horizon: Minimum horizon enforced by task selection: tasks whose shortest known solution has at least 8 turns on ALFWorld and 20 turns on the long environment (assumption: this drops about a third of ALFWorld).
regime.model_band: Qwen3-8B (2605.27881's default) and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (the GiGPO and ECPO lineage); one size each, so the table is not confounded by scale (2603.21972 found algorithm effects reverse between 1.5B and 7B).
regime.decision_density: Each environment's decision density $\rho$ (2606.22164) is measured once from counterfactual branching on 200 trajectories and reported as the x-coordinate of the plot.

spec.matched_compute: Per training run a fixed budget of sampled tokens $T$ and environment steps $E$, counting branches, sibling rollouts, critic forward and backward passes and judge calls (assumption: $T$ set to what flat GRPO with group 8 uses for 300 optimizer steps; branching recipes therefore see fewer root prompts). Wall-clock on the same hardware is logged as the second axis. A recipe that needs an external judge model is charged its tokens.
spec.matched_dose: Dose is the number of tokens with non-zero advantage entering the optimizer and the number of optimizer steps. Recipes that zero out routine steps (SCOPE, ProVer, CRR at selected steps) reduce the dose; each such recipe gets a second arm in which the removed steps keep the flat GRPO advantage, so a gain from targeting is separated from a gain from dropping examples (checklist, Comparisons: 'is the comparison measuring dose or credit?').
controls: Flat GRPO with group 8 (production default) and group 32 at the same token budget $T$ (strongest cheap incumbent: more siblings for free credit).
Shuffled credit: the recipe's own per-step weights permuted across steps within each trajectory, marginal-matched (same mean and spread), the control of CL-W43-06.
Placebo critic: the recipe's critic trained on returns from a different environment's trajectories, same architecture and budget.
Entropy-only credit: step weight proportional to the policy's mean token entropy on that step, the content-free targeting rule.
Pass-rate bands: tasks binned by the initial policy's pass rate over 16 samples into $[0, 0.2)$, $[0.2, 0.8)$, $[0.8, 1]$; every gain reported by band.
First-two-thirds split: credit quality (correlation with counterfactual return difference) reported separately for the first two thirds and the last third of each trajectory.
metrics: Success rate at the matched budget $T$ and at 0.5 $T$ and 2 $T$ (the curve, not one point), 3 seeds.
Credit quality: Spearman correlation between the recipe's step advantage and the counterfactual return difference from 4 branch rollouts at 200 held-out decision points, by trajectory third.
Stability: fraction of runs whose success drops more than 10 points from its peak before the budget ends.
Cost: GPU-hours and wall-clock per run, critic memory.
spec.single_plot: Gain over compute-matched flat GRPO (group 8) in success points, on the y-axis, against the environment's decision density $\rho$ on the x-axis, one marker per recipe per environment with its 3-seed band, the group-32 incumbent drawn as a horizontal line per environment and each recipe's shuffled-credit control drawn as a hollow marker. A recipe whose filled marker is inside its hollow marker's band is dead at that $\rho$.

preregistered_expectation.expected: Judgment probability 0.5. At matched compute, the large flat group absorbs at least half of every critic-free recipe's published gain on ALFWorld and WebShop; the critic-free hindsight recipes do not beat their shuffled control in the first two thirds of trajectories (CL-W43-06's parked claim); the stabilized critics (EasyPPO, Odysseus-style turn critic, SCALE) and the counterfactual recipes (CRR, TWICE) keep a gain of 5 or more points only on the long environment where $\rho$ is lowest; on the high pass-rate band no recipe beats flat GRPO.
preregistered_expectation.field_assumes: That step-level credit beats trajectory-level credit on long horizons generally; 2605.27881 already found 'the simplest outcome-based approach achieves competitive or superior performance in most settings' and that process credit 'can over-correct', at a 4-turn horizon; 2603.21972 found exploration variants help only at 1.5B; Odysseus found critic-free methods fail at 100 turns.
preregistered_expectation.would_change: If the expected result holds: every credit paper reports against group-32 flat GRPO at matched tokens and against its shuffled control, by band; training teams spend the critic's compute on group size except on low-$\rho$ environments. If a critic-free recipe beats its shuffled control and group-32 on all three environments by more than 5 points: that estimator becomes the default and the critic question is closed for this horizon band.

breakdown: Main grid: 14 recipe arms x 3 environments x 2 models x 3 seeds = 252 runs.

Controls: group-8, group-32, shuffled (per recipe family, 4), placebo critic (2), entropy-only (1) = 9 arms x 3 environments x 2 models x 3 seeds = 162 runs; shuffled arms share rollouts with their recipe where the estimator is post hoc.
Budget curve: 6 arms x 3 environments x 1 model x 3 seeds at 0.5 $T$ and 2 $T$ = 108 runs.
Credit-quality branching: 200 decision points x 4 branches x 3 environments x 14 recipes, inference only: 200 GPU-hours.
assumptions: 24 GPU-hours per training run on ALFWorld and WebShop (8 H100 for 3 hours at the 8B scale under verl with vLLM rollouts) and 72 on the long environment; weighted mean 40 GPU-hours per run; 522 runs x 40 = 20,900 at face value, reduced to about 14,000 because shuffled and dose arms reuse rollouts; the pilot measures the per-run cost and rescales.
If the per-run cost is 2x higher the total is 28,000; the reopen trigger is set at 14,000 and the first lab run should be the long environment only (one third of the total).

consumers: Every step-credit and critic paper in the lane (Gate 3 community-wide): report against compute-matched group-32 GRPO and the shuffled control by pass-rate band and decision density.
RL training teams (Narasimhan route, any RL group): whether to pay for a critic and on which environments.
Environment builders: decision density $\rho$ as a reported property of an agent environment.
Theorists: the $\rho^{-1/2}$ prediction of 2606.22164 tested across recipes rather than in a toy.
spec.why_not_run: Each recipe paper compares to flat GRPO at its own group size on ALFWorld and WebShop with 1.5B to 7B models and no compute matching; branching and counterfactual recipes double rollouts and report the gain per optimizer step. The two controlled studies are narrow by their own account: 2605.27881 'we cannot cover all existing credit assignment algorithms' and runs at most 4 tool turns; 2603.21972 varies exploration (DAPO, ARPO), not credit, on one environment. The shuffled-credit control appears in no paper in the lane (CL-W43-06 was parked on exactly that absence). A recipe author has no incentive to run the control that can zero their result, and the grid costs a lab's quarter. The lane publishes 4.5 papers a week, so each new recipe is compared to a baseline two months stale.
spec.enabling_piece: verl as a shared stack with four credit methods already re-implemented (2605.27881, 2026-05-27); decision density as a measurable environment property (2606.22164, 2026-06-20); forkable executable environments that make counterfactual credit computable (CRR 2609.33875, 2026-09-27); and the twin-world noise keying (2610.31544, 2026-10-22) that gives the credit-quality metric a low-variance ground truth.

publication_rate_per_week.method: Unique arXiv API hits in the last 8 weeks (2026-09-07 to 2026-11-01) whose title names credit assignment, critics, value functions, step- or turn-level advantages, process rewards or PPO/GRPO variants for agents: 36 papers / 8 weeks; 138 in 12 months by the same rule (22 in October 2026).

closest_comparisons.title: Retrieval, Reward, and Training Protocols: What Matters in Training Search Agents?
closest_comparisons.what_it_has: Four credit strategies (Search-R1 outcome-only, GiGPO, IGPO, Tree-GRPO) re-implemented on one GRPO objective in one verl codebase; three base models; 9,000 training instances; five QA test sets; a process evaluation of search behaviour; released checkpoints.
closest_comparisons.lacks: Horizon capped at 4 tool-call turns, so it is not long-horizon; no critic-based arm (no PPO, no learned value); compute not matched (Tree-GRPO's branch rollouts and GiGPO's grouping are charged nothing; batch size fixed, not tokens); no shuffled or placebo control; no pass-rate bands; search QA only (exact match); its own limitation: 'Due to resource constraints, we cannot cover all existing credit assignment algorithms' and conclusions 'limited to local corpus-based search environments'.

closest_comparisons.title: Demystifying Reinforcement Learning for Long-Horizon Tool-Using Agents: A Comprehensive Recipe
closest_comparisons.what_it_has: Five axes (reward shaping, model scale 1.5B/3B/7B, data composition, algorithm, environment stability) on TravelPlanner with GRPO, group 8, 1K queries; GPU-hours per algorithm reported on 8 or 16 A100s; seven takeaways including that algorithm effects reverse with scale.
closest_comparisons.lacks: The algorithm axis is exploration (GRPO versus DAPO versus ARPO), not credit: no step-level estimator and no critic in the table; one environment; GPU-hours reported but not matched (ARPO's branching is allowed to cost more); no control arms; reward shaping compared as staged versus dense, which changes dose and credit together.

closest_comparisons.title: Odysseus (third-closest)
closest_comparisons.what_it_has: Seven variants (GRPO outcome and process, each with and without positive-advantage filtering, turn-level Reinforce++, PPO with a CNN critic, PPO with a turn-level CNN critic and filtering) on one Super Mario Land level with Qwen3-VL-8B at a fixed 0.38M training samples, at least two runs each.
closest_comparisons.lacks: One game level, dense game reward, a VLM; no group-size incumbent; no shuffled or placebo control; sample-matched but not token- or wall-clock-matched; no published step-credit recipe beyond GRPO variants.

scorecard.target_value: In print: 2605.27881 'the rapid growth of training methods has outpaced controlled comparison' and 'process-level credit assignment can over-correct agent behavior'; 2603.21972 'a practical recipe for scaling RL in complex, multi-turn environments remains elusive'; 2606.22164 'the cost of trajectory-level credit assignment ... is in fact governed by decision density'; 2609.36802 'the critic is also a major source of instability'. Who pays: every team training agents with RL deciding whether to run a critic; environment builders.

impact_ceiling.floor: The ALFWorld pilot (300 GPU-hours): one recipe against group-32 and its shuffled control; a note that fixes the baseline for the next GiGPO-descendant. Judgment p 0.5.
impact_ceiling.middle: The three-environment table at matched compute with the decision-density plot; adopted as the baseline protocol by one RL framework (verl's agent examples) and cited by the lane's recipe papers. Requires the 14,000 GPU-hours. Judgment p 0.3.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The plot settles when critics pay (by $\rho$ and band), changes the default recipe in two agent-RL frameworks and makes $\rho$ a reported environment property (community-wide Gate 3). Requires a lab room with the compute and a published environment with measured $\rho$. Judgment p 0.1.

scorecard.relevance: Narasimhan route (Odysseus, EasyPPO): direct, two of the recipes are theirs. Any RL group: direct. Industry: direct for training spend. Jacob's edge: the matched-compute design, the shuffled control and the correlation readout are statistics; the RL stack engineering is computer engineering; theoretical physics zero.
scorecard.kill_probe: The 300 GPU-hour ALFWorld pilot; dead if GiGPO beats group-32 and its shuffled control by more than 5 points with credit quality above 0.3 in the first two thirds.
scorecard.density_and_ownership: 138 keyword hits in 12 months, 36 in 8 weeks. Closest two: 2605.27881 and 2603.21972, limitation text quoted in closest_comparisons. Pre-window precedents: GiGPO 2505.10978 (anchor-state groups), flat GRPO (Shao et al. 2024, cited by every paper in the lane). The Narasimhan group owns Odysseus and EasyPPO and has the stack; the re-open test is asking whether they would host the table.
scorecard.why_now: Shared verl re-implementations, decision density, forkable environments and twin-world keying, May to October 2026.
scorecard.register: Definitive controlled comparison with a recipe consequence (critic or group size, by $\rho$). It is not a new estimator, not a theory of credit and not a benchmark.

preregistered_surprise.expected: Judgment probability 0.5. At matched compute, the large flat group absorbs at least half of every critic-free recipe's published gain on ALFWorld and WebShop; the critic-free hindsight recipes do not beat their shuffled control in the first two thirds of trajectories (CL-W43-06's parked claim); the stabilized critics (EasyPPO, Odysseus-style turn critic, SCALE) and the counterfactual recipes (CRR, TWICE) keep a gain of 5 or more points only on the long environment where $\rho$ is lowest; on the high pass-rate band no recipe beats flat GRPO.
preregistered_surprise.field_assumes: That step-level credit beats trajectory-level credit on long horizons generally; 2605.27881 already found 'the simplest outcome-based approach achieves competitive or superior performance in most settings' and that process credit 'can over-correct', at a 4-turn horizon; 2603.21972 found exploration variants help only at 1.5B; Odysseus found critic-free methods fail at 100 turns.
preregistered_surprise.would_change: If the expected result holds: every credit paper reports against group-32 flat GRPO at matched tokens and against its shuffled control, by band; training teams spend the critic's compute on group size except on low-$\rho$ environments. If a critic-free recipe beats its shuffled control and group-32 on all three environments by more than 5 points: that estimator becomes the default and the critic question is closed for this horizon band.

identifiability: Random given: one environment at a pinned version, one seed for the environment and the sampler, one stack; ALFWorld and WebShop are deterministic after the action, so within-group return variance is the policy's sampling, and the counterfactual return difference at a decision point is identified by branching with the same downstream noise (TWICE) or by averaging 4 branches. The gain over flat GRPO is a property of (recipe, environment, model, $T$, seed set). Credit quality is a correlation with a verifier-computed return difference, not a judge. Decision density $\rho$ is a property of (environment, initial policy) and is reported with that conditioning.

reopen_trigger: lab compute of >= 2200 GPU-hours and a shared harness (one MJCF task set that loads unchanged into MJX, MuJoCo Warp, Newton, Genesis and Isaac Lab behind one PPO code path, about three person-months)
title: Reference return versus solver budget: the compute-matched comparison of shipped fidelity settings across five GPU engines on three contact-rich tasks
statement: Load one MJCF specification of three contact-rich tasks into MJX, MuJoCo Warp, Newton, Genesis and Isaac Lab, train one PPO code path at a grid of solver iteration caps $k$, time steps $h$ and contact softness $\sigma$ around each engine's shipped default under a fixed GPU-hour budget $B$ (and, in a second arm, a fixed environment-step count $N$), evaluate every policy under its engine's converged setting and one other engine's converged setting, compute the transfer loss $\Delta = 1 - R_{\text{ref}}/R_{\text{train}}$ and the exploit share $\rho_{\text{ex}}$, against a shuffled-budget control, a friction-randomization placebo and PolySim-style engine mixing, and validate the reference on one task against GAUGE's motion-capture data.
claim: At matched training compute, the shipped solver budgets of GPU physics engines sit below the throughput-versus-reference-return envelope on contact-rich manipulation, the knee of the envelope differs more across engines than their published fidelity scores do, and the policy's in-engine return hides the loss because it rises as the budget falls.
trick: Train the same policy at several solver budgets on five engines for the same number of GPU-hours, then score every policy under the converged physics instead of the physics it was trained in.
why_now: One MJCF file now runs on five GPU engines (Newton 1.3 and GAUGE's three-engine run, 2026-08; MJX and Warp share the format), GPUSimBench fixed the batch non-determinism protocol (2026-07), and the per-step reference audit is this pipeline's instrument (CL-W43-01, 2026-10); the lane's two measurer papers both stopped at defaults with no policy in the loop.

killing_experiment.design: One engine (MuJoCo Warp), one task (peg insertion), the iteration axis only ($k_0/2$ to $8k_0$), 3 seeds, compute-matched at $B = 4$ GPU-hours, every policy re-evaluated at $8k_0$; plus the exploit share on the visited states.
killing_experiment.kills_if: Reference return at $k_0$ is within 5% of reference return at $8k_0$ with overlapping 3-seed bands and $\rho_{\text{ex}}$ does not separate the $k_0/2$ policies from the $8k_0$ policies: the shipped cap is on the envelope for the lane's hardest contact task, CL-W43-01's exploit claim fails its own kill test on one engine, and the cross-engine table is a verification service, not a paper.

spec.problem: Across five GPU engines, how much transferable policy return do the shipped fidelity settings (solver iteration cap, time step, contact softness) give up at matched training compute, and which knob, on which task class, sets the knee?

recipes.name: Isaac Lab at shipped defaults (production default per GPUSimBench's recommendation)
recipes.trick: PhysX rigid bodies on the GPU with the engine's default solver iterations, time step and contact parameters; GPUSimBench calls it the balanced default.

recipes.name: MJX / MuJoCo Warp / MuJoCo Playground at defaults
recipes.trick: MuJoCo's soft-constraint contact model on JAX or Warp at the shipped iteration cap and time step; MJX scored second-lowest trajectory error in GPUSimBench's inclined-plane test.

recipes.name: Newton 1.3 (MuJoCo solver in Warp) and Genesis at defaults
recipes.trick: Two more GPU engines, measured out of the box by GAUGE against motion-capture trajectories with calibrated material parameters.

recipes.name: Kamino (Newton)
recipes.trick: An ADMM constrained-optimisation solver in Warp for closed kinematic loops and heterogeneous batched worlds; its iteration count is a knob the paper exposes.

recipes.name: PolySim (pre-window precedent)
recipes.trick: Train one policy across IsaacGym, IsaacSim and Genesis at once so the controller cannot fit any single engine's contact assumptions; tested on MuJoCo as the unseen engine.

recipes.name: MFPG-PPO
recipes.trick: Use cheap low-fidelity simulator rollouts only as a control variate for the high-fidelity policy gradient, so the bias stays out and the variance drops; run in GPU-parallel simulation and on a robot.

recipes.name: Bundled Contact Gradients
recipes.trick: Keep contact stiff for fidelity but smooth the gradient locally at contacts by randomized bundling, so first-order policy learning does not blow up as stiffness rises.

recipes.name: All You Need Is Low Fidelity
recipes.trick: A deliberately stateless, wake-free fluid model plus two identifications is enough for a fish controller that transfers zero-shot; fidelity bought where identification says it matters.

recipes.name: CLASH
recipes.trick: Distil a collision surrogate from MuJoCo, then identify a few contact parameters and a residual from ten real collisions and plug it back into the engine.

recipes.name: ConCent
recipes.trick: Reproduce the contact event sequence and the local contact dynamics from one demonstration before training, because contact fidelity is the necessary condition for transfer.

recipes.name: few-shot neural differentiable simulator
recipes.trick: Calibrate an analytical engine on little real data, generate synthetic contacts, and train a mesh GNN with surrogate collision gradients.

recipes.name: Contact-Aware Neural Dynamics
recipes.trick: Treat the engine as a prior and learn a tactile-informed residual that corrects its states where contacts are discontinuous.

recipes.name: Real-IKEA
recipes.trick: Collision meshes scored by surface deviation and resistance-calibrated damping and friction; an RL policy finds robust behaviours only with the accurate assets.

recipes.name: Tac2Real
recipes.trick: A preconditioned nonlinear conjugate-gradient IPC contact solver on multi-GPU for visuotactile RL, with a systematic domain-gap alignment.

recipes.name: proprioceptive distribution matching
recipes.trick: Adapt the simulator (parameters, action deltas, residual actuators) by matching distributions of joint observations and actions, no time alignment needed.

recipes.name: transfer budget allocation
recipes.trick: In a sim-to-sim pendulum, a few identification rollouts beat wide randomization; measurement does most of the work.

recipes.name: GPUSimBench (instrument)
recipes.trick: Throughput, memory, one inclined-plane fidelity test and batch-position / run-to-run variability for seven GPU engines at one time step.

recipes.name: GAUGE (instrument)
recipes.trick: Motion-capture-grounded trajectory error for three engines and video world models on 22 task families at engine defaults.

recipes.name: muscle-driven fidelity benchmark
recipes.trick: Two imitation pipelines (HyFyDy, MuJoCo/MyoSim) compared on muscle activations and metabolic cost, not only kinematics.

recipes.name: SAPU (pre-window precedent)
recipes.trick: Interpenetration is unavoidable and exploited; drop episodes over 1 mm overlap and down-weight the rest.

spec.harness: One task specification in MJCF for three contact-rich tasks, loaded unchanged into MJX, MuJoCo Warp, Newton (MuJoCo solver and Kamino), Genesis and Isaac Lab (MJCF import), with PolySim's simulator-router idea (2510.01708: friction, actuator gains, gravity and integration step harmonised) extended to five engines; one PPO implementation (rsl_rl-style, one code path, engine behind a step() interface); one evaluation reference per task: the same engine's converged setting (iterations x8, time step /4, hard contact) plus one cross-engine reference, so 'transferable return' is defined without a robot and then validated on one task against GAUGE's real rigid-body trajectories.

regime.tasks: Quadruped rough-terrain locomotion (Go2 or ANYmal), in-hand cube reorientation (Allegro or LEAP), peg-in-hole insertion (Franka); assumption: one task per class where the lane's literature claims exploitation (SAPU for insertion, GPUSimBench's inclined plane for contact).
regime.knob_grid: Solver iterations $k \in \{k_0/2, k_0, 2k_0, 4k_0, 8k_0\}$ where $k_0$ is each engine's shipped cap; time step $h \in \{h_0, h_0/2, h_0/4\}$; contact softness $\sigma \in \{\sigma_0, \text{hard}\}$ where 'hard' is the engine's stiffest stable setting; full grid on the iteration axis at $(h_0, \sigma_0)$ and one-at-a-time on the other two (assumption: 5 + 2 + 1 = 8 settings per engine per task, with the converged corner as the ninth).
regime.model_band: One PPO policy architecture and hyperparameter set per task across engines (assumption: the Isaac Lab defaults for that task, frozen before the first run).
regime.forced_regime: Every arm trains to the same wall-clock GPU budget (compute-matched) and, in a second arm, to the same environment-step count (dose-matched), because a higher iteration cap lowers throughput and the two arms separate 'fidelity costs samples' from 'fidelity costs time'.

spec.matched_compute: GPU-hours per training run fixed at $B$ (assumption: $B = 2$ GPU-hours on one H100 for locomotion at 4096 environments, the field's typical budget; $B = 4$ for manipulation). Throughput (steps per second) is logged per setting so the frontier can be re-read at any budget.
spec.matched_dose: Environment steps fixed at $N$ (assumption: $N$ = the steps the default setting reaches in $B$); higher-fidelity arms then take up to 8x longer. Both arms are reported; the plot uses the compute-matched arm.
controls: Shuffled budget: per-environment iteration count drawn at random each step with the same mean as $k_0$ (tests whether the mean solver budget or the cap is what matters; also the systems lever's premise).
Placebo: friction and mass domain randomization at $k_0$ (the field's standard answer to the reality gap), same compute.
PolySim-style engine mixing at defaults, same compute (the published cross-engine recipe as an arm).

Exploit audit: per-step physics residual $d_t = \lVert F_{\text{ref}}(x_t, u_t) - x_{t+1} \rVert$ on the states each trained policy visits, with $F_{\text{ref}}$ the converged step of the same engine, and the exploit share $\rho_{\text{ex}} = \sum_t r_t \mathbf{1}[d_t > \kappa] / \sum_t r_t$ (themes.yaml L5 instrument; $\kappa$ calibrated on converged-trained policies).

Real validation on one task: the trained policies' contact trajectories scored against GAUGE's rigid-body motion-capture data (2608.05948) so 'converged reference' is checked against reality at least once.
Seeds: 3 per cell; pass-rate bands replaced by task-difficulty bands (terrain level, cube goal angle, hole clearance).
metrics: In-engine return $R_{\text{train}}$ (what the paper would report).
Reference return $R_{\text{ref}}$: the same policy evaluated under the converged setting of its own engine and under one other engine's converged setting.
Transfer loss $\Delta = 1 - R_{\text{ref}} / R_{\text{train}}$ and the exploit share $\rho_{\text{ex}}$.
Throughput in environment steps per second per setting; GPU-hours to reach 90% of the setting's final return.
spec.single_plot: Reference return $R_{\text{ref}}$ against training GPU-hours, one curve per (engine, iteration cap) at the shipped time step and contact setting, one panel per task, with each engine's shipped default marked by a filled point; the upper envelope is the throughput-versus-verified-fidelity frontier the lane names, and a default that sits below the envelope at its own budget is a shipped setting that trades physics for speed.

preregistered_expectation.expected: Judgment probability 0.5. In-engine return is flat or rising as the cap falls (the policy adapts to the artifacts), reference return falls, and the knee sits between $2k_0$ and $4k_0$ for insertion and in-hand tasks and at or below $k_0$ for locomotion; the knee differs more across engines than their GPUSimBench or GAUGE fidelity scores differ (CL-W43-J04); the time step matters more than the cap for locomotion and less for manipulation; the shuffled-budget arm matches the cap arm at the same mean, so the systems lever (iteration-level scheduling) is admissible; the exploit share $\rho_{\text{ex}}$ separates coarse-trained from converged-trained policies on at least two tasks (CL-W43-01's kill test).
preregistered_expectation.field_assumes: That shipped defaults are adequate and the reality gap is a parameter problem solved by randomization or identification; GPUSimBench recommends Isaac Lab as the balanced default on throughput and one inclined-plane test, GAUGE measures engines at defaults, PolySim treats engines as domains to randomize over, and no paper in the window sweeps the cap or the step as the treatment.
preregistered_expectation.would_change: If the expected result holds: engine teams ship task-class presets rather than one default, every robot-RL paper reports its iteration cap and time step with a reference-return check, and the iteration-level scheduler has a measured headroom. If defaults sit on the envelope on all three tasks: the lane's exploit claim (CL-W43-01) is refuted for shipped settings and the audit is a verification tool, not a headline.

breakdown: Training grid: 5 engines x 3 tasks x 9 settings x 3 seeds = 405 runs, compute-matched arm.
Dose-matched arm on the iteration axis only: 5 engines x 3 tasks x 5 settings x 3 seeds = 225 runs at up to 8x the default's wall-clock (mean 3x).
Controls (shuffled budget, randomization placebo, engine mixing): 3 x 5 x 3 x 3 = 135 runs.
Reference re-simulation audits and cross-engine evaluation: 200 GPU-hours (inference only, converged settings).
GAUGE validation on one task: 20 GPU-hours.
assumptions: Compute-matched runs cost $B$ by construction: 405 x (2 or 4) = 1,080 GPU-hours.
Dose-matched runs: 225 x 3 x 2 = 1,350 GPU-hours at the mean slowdown; reduced to about 900 by stopping at 90% of final return.

Total about 2,200 GPU-hours; the engineering cost (one MJCF task set loaded into five engines with harmonised contact parameters, one PPO code path) is the real cost, about three person-months, and is the reason the harness is in the reopen trigger.

consumers: Engine teams (MuJoCo Warp, Newton, Genesis, Isaac Lab): per-task-class presets for the cap and the step; the two measurer papers already address them.
Every group training policies in GPU simulators (Gate 3 community-wide in robotics RL): report the cap, the step and a reference-return check.
Sim-to-real papers: whether identification and randomization are being spent on an artifact the solver budget created.
The systems route: the measured per-world iteration headroom that iteration-level scheduling needs (themes.yaml kill test 2).
spec.why_not_run: No shared task specification runs unchanged on five engines (PolySim's router covers three and harmonises only what the engines expose; MuJoCo Playground covers MJX and Warp only), so the cross-engine harness is three person-months before the first run. The two measurer papers measured engines at defaults with no policy in the loop (GPUSimBench: one time step 0.01 s, 'two scalability scenes and one contact-rich real-world-matched experiment, all on a single hardware and software stack'; GAUGE: 'all other settings remain at their defaults without task-specific fine-tuning'). Engine teams' incentive is throughput at defaults, and a recipe paper's incentive is transfer on its own task. The reference-return readout without a robot is this pipeline's instrument (CL-W43-01) and is not yet in print. Publication rate is low (about 0.3 recipe papers a week), so the race window is long, and the blocker is the harness, not the compute.
spec.enabling_piece: Newton 1.3 and MuJoCo Warp share MuJoCo's MJCF model format with MJX, and Genesis and Isaac Lab import MJCF, so one task file can run on five GPU engines for the first time (Newton's public release and GAUGE's three-engine run, 2026-08); GPUSimBench (2026-07) documents batch-position non-determinism, which fixes the seed protocol; and the per-step audit from this pipeline (CL-W43-01, 2026-10) supplies the reference-return readout.

publication_rate_per_week.method: Hand-curated from the arXiv API hits: 14 papers in the 12 months to 2026-11-01 that treat simulator fidelity as the lever (contact-model recipes, multi-engine training, multi-fidelity gradients, engine measurers), 0 that sweep the iteration cap or time step as the treatment; 14 / 52 weeks = 0.27. The keyword count (titles naming simulators, physics engines, fidelity, contact or sim-to-real with RL) is 86 / 52 = 1.7 per week and is the upper bound.

closest_comparisons.title: GPUSimBench: Towards Scalable and Reliable GPU-Accelerated Simulators in Embodied AI
closest_comparisons.what_it_has: Seven GPU engines (ManiSkill, Genesis, Madrona, MuJoCo Warp, MJX, MuJoCo Playground, Isaac Lab) on one workstation: throughput and memory on a cube array and a Franka scene, an inclined-plane collision test against a real apparatus (earth-mover distance per engine), and batch-position versus run-to-run variability types; a decision guide naming Isaac Lab the balanced default.
closest_comparisons.lacks: Every engine at its shipped settings with one unified time step of 0.01 s and no sweep of solver iterations, time step or contact softness; no policy trained, so no return and no transfer; one contact-rich fidelity test; its own limitation: 'two scalability scenes and one contact-rich real-world-matched experiment, all on a single hardware and software stack ... the reported performance and variability may change across different GPUs, drivers, and simulator versions'.

closest_comparisons.title: GAUGE: A Measurement-Grounded Benchmark for Physical Fidelity in Simulation Engines and Video World Models
closest_comparisons.what_it_has: Isaac Sim 6.0, Genesis 1.12 and Newton 1.3 on 14 motion-capture-grounded tasks (rigid bodies, textiles, volumetric deformables) with calibrated material parameters, trajectory error per engine, 180 Hz simulation, and a parallel video-world-model track.
closest_comparisons.lacks: Engines at defaults by design ('all other settings remain at their defaults without task-specific fine-tuning'); no solver-budget or time-step axis; no policy, so fidelity is never tied to return or to throughput; its limitations section names material ranges and fluids, not solver settings; three engines, not MJX or Warp.

closest_comparisons.title: PolySim (third-closest)
closest_comparisons.what_it_has: One humanoid tracking policy trained across IsaacGym, IsaacSim and Genesis with a router that harmonises friction, actuator gains, gravity and integration step; 14 ASAP motions; MuJoCo as the unseen test engine; single-engine and mixed arms compared on success and tracking error.
closest_comparisons.lacks: Engines at harmonised defaults, no fidelity knob swept; the comparison is engine mixing versus single engine, not setting versus setting; compute per arm not matched (mixed arms run more engines); one task family; no audit of what the policies exploit.

scorecard.target_value: In print: GPUSimBench 'the underlying trade-offs between parallel efficiency, physical fidelity, and execution determinism remain largely unexamined'; GAUGE 'existing evaluations of physical fidelity are often conducted in isolation'; PolySim 'the sim-to-real gap ... fundamentally arises from simulator inductive bias'; Bundled Contact Gradients 'softened contact models, often at the expense of physical fidelity'. Who pays: every group training policies in GPU simulators, every engine team choosing a default cap.

impact_ceiling.floor: The one-engine, one-task iteration sweep with reference return (90 GPU-hours): the first number on what a shipped cap costs in transferable return; cited by the next engine release note. Judgment p 0.5.
impact_ceiling.middle: The five-engine, three-task table and the envelope plot; engine teams ship per-task presets and robot-RL papers report cap and step. Requires the harness (three person-months) and 2,200 GPU-hours. Judgment p 0.3.
impact_ceiling.ceiling: The table plus the GAUGE validation becomes the verification standard for GPU simulators (community-wide Gate 3), with the iteration-level scheduler as the systems follow-on measured against the headroom the table reveals. Requires a robotics lab room and an engine team's cooperation. Judgment p 0.1.

Jacob's edge: numerics and convergence (theoretical physics), GPU scheduling (computer engineering); no mechanical engineering is assumed.

scorecard.density_and_ownership: 14 fidelity-as-lever papers in 12 months, 0 knob sweeps; 86 keyword hits. If defaults sit on the envelope on all three tasks: the lane's exploit claim (CL-W43-01) is refuted for shipped settings and the audit is a verification tool, not a headline.

identifiability: Random given: one engine at a pinned version and driver, one task file, one seed for the sampler and the environment, batch position fixed (GPUSimBench documents batch-position variability, so returns are reported per batch slot). $R_{\text{train}}$ and $R_{\text{ref}}$ are properties of (policy, engine, setting); $\Delta$ conditions on the policy's own training setting.
